articles.title_orig: Trump welcomes China's Xi for state dinner at White House after touting "truly great friendship"
articles.title_zh: Trump welcomes China's Xi for state dinner at White House after touting "truly great friendship"
articles.content_orig:
During remarks at the White House state dinner, Chinese President Xi Jinping said he and President Trump had "sincere and in-depth exchanges" earlier in the day, and "reached common understanding on many issues."
"This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability," Xi said through a translator.
Xi did not specify what the two leaders discussed or whether they struck any new agreements, but trade and AI were widely believed to be agenda items. The U.S. and China agreed earlier this week to extend a truce on tariffs for two months, forestalling another trade war for now, though the two countries have not struck a broader deal. The two sides are also rivals on advanced AI, with Mr. Trump arguing for light regulations in order to outpace China. Other major pressure points include China's relationships with Iran and Russia and the future of Taiwan.
Xi briefly recounted the history of U.S.-China ties. He pointed to President George Washington's purchase of Chinese porcelain , the two countries' cooperation during World War II and President Richard Nixon's moves to normalize relations with the People's Republic of China.
He said the U.S. and China have come to "another historic juncture," and argued the two countries' ambitions "can surely be mutually reinforcing."
"China and the United States must act as responsible major countries, meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other," he said.
President Trump gave his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, a large bald eagle sculpture at the end of his brief remarks at Thursday's state dinner.
During a speech recognizing U.S.-China ties, President Trump offered Chinese President Xi Jinping and other guests a "special treat" — a peek at the construction site for the White House ballroom.
"In honor of you, you'll be the first people to step foot on that," the president said, suggesting guests could take a look after the evening's entertainment wraps up.
Mr. Trump speaks about the ballroom frequently, weighing in on design decisions and casting the massive, controversial project as part of his legacy. He has often argued it will allow the White House to host larger state dinners.
"I can tell you that tonight, if we had it, we would've had way more than a thousand people [at the dinner] with standing room only," he said.
In remarks at Thursday's state dinner, President Trump called for the U.S. and China to "continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."
Mr. Trump, who has long touted his warm personal relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping, called Xi and his wife "truly outstanding, amazing people."
"As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure," Mr. Trump said. "And we've never gotten along better."
Mr. Trump traced the history of U.S.-China relations back to the European explorers who arrived at the American continent while scouring the Atlantic Ocean for new routes to China. He also pointed to early U.S. commercial ties with China, saying the two countries have exchanged "goods, knowledge, customs and ideas."
During a toast to Xi, he said: "May all of our people know a future of harmony, peace and success."
The White House released the invite list for Thursday's state dinner, which includes high-level government officials and several of the world's wealthiest tech executives.
Among the notable people on the guest list are Vice President JD Vance and several Cabinet-level officials: Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and CIA Director John Ratcliffe.
Mr. Trump's children – Ivanka, Eric and Tiffany – also got invites.
The world's richest person, Elon Musk, is on the list. NVIDIA's Jensen Huang, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Apple's Tim Cook, Google's Sundar Pichai, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and TikTok investor Jeff Yass also got invites.
Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison is also attending. (Paramount Skydance is the parent company of CBS News.)
President Trump and first lady Melania Trump walked out of the White House's North Portico shortly after 7 p.m. Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, then arrived in a car and posed for photos with the Trumps before walking inside.
Mr. Trump did not answer shouted questions about Taiwan, Iran or whether Mr. Trump asked Xi to free imprisoned pro-democracy Hong Kong media tycoon Jimmy Lai .
A group of demonstrators was audible from the White House's North Portico ahead of Thursday evening's state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping.
A woman with a megaphone led a crowd of protesters through chants like: "Xi Jinping, You're Not Welcome," "Free Hong Kong," "Keep Taiwan Free" and "China Sponsors Genocide."
Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sanchez, have arrived at the White House state dinner.
Several minutes later, fellow tech titan Michael Dell and his wife, Susan, walked into the event.
Other high-profile executives are expected to attend the dinner, including the CEOs of Nvidia, Qualcomm and OpenAI, CBS News has previously reported.
Republican Sen. Thom Tillis questioned President Trump's judgment in hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state dinner at the White House this week, saying he's "worried about the trend of spending more time with despots and less time with democratic leaders of nations."
"It's a WTF moment," the retiring North Carolina senator said in an interview with "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil on Thursday about Mr. Trump's red-carpet rollout for Xi compared to the reception that some U.S. allies like Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy have received.
"It's not that Xi Jinping is coming here to learn how to become a democratic, capitalist nation. Xi Jinping is trying to understand how his opposition will ultimately embrace their worldview," he said.
President Trump took to Truth Social to voice his frustration that CNN and MS NOW didn't air the arrival ceremony for Xi, saying it was "made for television." Other networks, including CBS News, also didn't air the arrival ceremony.
CNN and MS NOW, along with Politico, were banned from the White House last week. While a federal judge ordered the outlets' access to be restored, it's not clear whether CNN will be allowed to participate in the White House television pool . And as long as CNN lacks a guarantee that it will be in the regular pool rotation again, the other four networks that make up the pool also aren't participating.
Members of the pool — NBC, ABC, CBS, CNN and Fox News — are declining to provide video coverage of the president until the White House guarantees it will let CNN back in. Some networks chose not to air the government's feed of the event, since the television pool was not present. News outlets are still reporting on the event itself.
The arrival ceremony for Xi was not open to all media, but only to the pool. ABC News was the representative for the pool on Thursday.
"CNN and MSDNC, to show you how fake they are, today refused to cover one of the Biggest and Most Beautiful Events to take place in many years, the arrival at the White House of the Highly Respected President of China, Xi Jinping, and his beautiful wife, Madam Peng," Mr. Trump wrote. "The event was magnificent — Actually made for Television but, because they're Fake News, and because they knew how good it would be, they didn't want credit to be given to "TRUMP," they refused to be there. That's why they have such poor Ratings. Tonight's State Dinner at the White House, for President Xi, will be spectacular! The Media will be in attendance."

articles.title_orig: Woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her aged 13 says claims were false
articles.title_zh: Woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her aged 13 says claims were false
articles.content_orig:
Jay-Z, pictured at the Met Gala in May 2026, previously hit out at the "frivolous, fictitious and appalling allegations"
A woman who accused Jay-Z of raping her when she was 13 has formally said her allegation was untrue.
The unnamed woman filed a lawsuit in 2024 claiming she had been drugged and raped by Jay-Z, real name Shawn Carter, and Sean "Diddy" Combs at a party after the MTV Video Music Awards in 2000.
The stars denied the allegation and she dropped the lawsuit last year. Carter then sued her and her lawyers.
In a statement filed in that case on Thursday, she wrote: "Shawn 'Jay-Z' Carter never raped me. I have never met or spoken to Mr. Carter. Mr. Carter never engaged in any inappropriate conduct toward me whatsoever."
The woman, known in court documents by the pseudonym Jane Doe, also said: "My claims that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me while a third celebrity, [name redacted] watched are false. There is no truth to any of my claims against Mr Carter.
"I understand my false accusations have caused Mr Carter immense pain, suffering, and damage that can never be fully undone."
Carter had vehemently denied the accusations, saying they were a "blackmail attempt" and describing them as "frivolous, fictitious and appalling allegations".
When the accuser dropped her case in February 2025, the rapper, who is married to singer BeyoncÃ©, said: "The trauma that my wife, my children, loved ones and I have endured can never be dismissed."
The woman, from Alabama, has now been removed from Carter's lawsuit.
She said she had not received any money from the rap superstar or anyone acting on his behalf, and had not been paid to make her latest declaration.
The rapper is still suing the woman's former lawyers, led by Tony Buzbee.
In a statement to Rolling Stone , external , which first reported Jane Doe's new declaration, Buzbee said he had not seen it.
He said: "We have multiple lawyers (at least four) who dealt with Ms Doe long before she met me. She gave the exact same story to each. If for some reason now she is claiming she lied to us and the court, that's new information."
When Carter filed his lawsuit against the woman and her lawyers in February 2025, Buzbee claimed at the time that Carter's investigators had "repeatedly harassed, threatened and harangued this poor woman for weeks, trying to intimidate her and make her recant her story".
In her new declaration, the woman said: "I never received any threat from Mr Carter or anyone acting on his behalf."
Setting out the events that led to her allegation, the woman said she saw an advert on Facebook in September or October 2024 looking for people who might have sexual assault claims against Combs. "The ad triggered memories of being raped when I was 13 years old," she said.
She was contacted by a law firm but was not provided with a draft of the lawsuit containing her allegations and did not authorise it before it was filed in October 2024, she said.
She also said Buzbee and other lawyers acting on her behalf filed it "without conducting any independent investigation, background inquiry, or due diligence, and without obtaining any corroboration of the allegations".
She said: "The October Complaint alleges that Mr Carter and Mr Combs raped me when I was a minor while an unnamed celebrity watched. As discussed above, these allegations were false."
Buzbee also represents numerous other people who have made allegations against Combs.
Combs denied Jane Doe's claims, which his lawyer described at the time as one of a number of civil cases "pushed forward by an attorney more focused on media headlines than legal merit".
The BBC has contacted Buzbee for comment.
In July 2025, Combs was convicted by a criminal court on prostitution-related charges involving his two ex-girlfriends, and is currently serving a four-year prison sentence.

articles.title_orig: Wisconsin police find dozens of partially clothed men in frat house basement in alleged hazing incident
articles.title_zh: Wisconsin police find dozens of partially clothed men in frat house basement in alleged hazing incident
articles.content_orig:
Two 20-year-olds were arrested after police were called to the scene of an alleged hazing incident where over two dozen young men were partially clothed and covered in liquids. Some of them were injured, police said.
The Madison Police Department said they received an anonymous tip about an event at the unaccredited Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity. When they arrived at the house, they found about 30 "partially clothed males covered in food, condiments and other liquids" in the basement. The room's thermostat was set to 81 degrees, police said.
Several of the men had "visible injuries consistent with being abused," police said.
The "vast majority" of the men were 18, police said.
A photo with the men's faces redacted shows the group in a dirty space with black walls and the Alpha Epsilon Pi letters painted on a piece of furniture.
Two people, identified by police as Brayden J. Klein and Samuel N. Vane, were arrested for hazing and disorderly conduct and taken to the Dane County Jail. The Madison Police Department said that the president and vice president of the fraternity were present and spoke to responding officers, but did not specify if Klein and Vane held those titles.
The men in the basement were escorted outside and checked for incapacitation and injuries.
"Several of these men had visible injuries consistent with being physically assaulted," police said.
No other charges have been announced in relation to the incident. An investigation remains ongoing, and those with information are asked to contact the Madison Police Department.
Alpha Epsilon Pi is an unrecognized and unaccredited student organization at the University of Wisconsin, police and the school said. The school said in a statement that because the chapter is still recognized by the national Alpha Epsilon Pi organization, it is legally allowed to operate as an unaffiliated fraternity chapter.
A spokesperson for the Alpha Epsilon Pi Headquarters said it takes the allegations concerning the Madison chapter "extremely seriously." The national organization plans to "cooperate fully" with the investigation, the spokesperson said, and members found responsible for criminal conduct will be expelled from the organization.
"Hazing is a betrayal of everything our fraternity stands for," the spokeperson said." There is no place for it in AEPi. No exceptions. No excuses. We educate our members about their responsibility to 'Be Your Brothers' Keeper.' This is not an optional value. It is a fundamental expectation of membership. Anyone who engages in hazing forfeits the privilege of being an AEPi brother."
The University of Wisconsin said it is also investigating the incident as it relates to its nonacademic misconduct process. Campus officials are providing support to affected students.
The Madison Police Department said that anyone whose safety is jeopardized during the Greek life recruitment process should contact authorities.

articles.title_orig: Treasury Yields Are Spiking. Where to Invest in the Bond Market Now.
articles.title_zh: Treasury Yields Are Spiking. Where to Invest in the Bond Market Now.
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Treasury yields rose on Friday as recent selling pressure intensified following hawkish Federal Reserve commentary and stronger-than-expected economic data.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note was up more than 4 basis points to 5.209% after reaching its highest rate since June 2007 on Thursday. The 30-year Treasury bond was higher by more than 5 basis points at 5.516% after surging to levels not seen since 2004. The 2-year note yield was up less than 1 basis point at 4.897%.
One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.
Investors also weighed a global bond sell-off this week as Japanese government bonds, U.K. gilts, German bunds and other eurozone bonds hit fresh highs. Eurozone and Japanese government bond yields edged lower on Friday.
Treasury yields have been driven higher by hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr, who said in a speech on Wednesday that "further policy adjustments" can be expected to bring inflation down to target. Other factors included stubbornly high oil prices and the purchasing managers' index report hitting its highest level in more than four years.
Traders were last pricing in a 66% chance of a rate hike in October, according to the CME FedWatch tool .
"Ahead, we think that there are enough rate hike fears discounted at this juncture, and certainly enough to take care of perceived inflation risks," ING's regional head of research for the Americas Padhraic Garvey and senior rates strategist Benjamin Schroeder wrote in a note on Friday.
"But, government bond yields are primed to remain under pressure on a pure debt dynamic theory, which translates into pressure for some re-widening in swap spreads, and especially in the 10yr area."
On Friday, durable goods orders in August came in relatively unchanged , while economists polled by Dow Jones had expected a decline of 0.3%. Additionally, consumer sentiment plummeted in September.

articles.title_orig: Nor’easter Could Bring Heavy Rain, Winds, and Flooding to East Coast
articles.title_zh: Nor’easter Could Bring Heavy Rain, Winds, and Flooding to East Coast
articles.content_orig:
Forecasters say up to 40 million people in multiple US states could be affected by the early season northeasterly storm
High winds and heavy rain were beginning to batter New England on Friday as a “significant” nor’easter, the first such storm of the fall, threatened to disrupt weekend plans for millions.
In the Pacific Ocean, meanwhile, three separate hurricanes, one threatening “ catastrophic flooding ”, including life-threatening flash floods, in Hawaii, were churning as a record-setting El Niño continued to amplify severe weather events on a global scale.
Forecasters said up to 40 million people across multiple US states could be affected by the early season northeasterly storm that was already lashing coastal areas of Rhode Island, Massachusetts, Connecticut and New York’s Long Island by Friday morning.
“Strong winds and rough seas along with a prolonged period of steady rain across the region are expected through this weekend,” the National Weather Service’s Boston office warned in a post on X , adding that rain could last until Monday.
“Beach erosion, coastal flooding, and wind damage including downed limbs and power outages are our main concerns.”
Areas farther inland were also bracing for the arrival of the storm, which has the potential to deliver hurricane force winds despite uncertainty over exactly where it will go.
The online AccuWeather service said winds of 40mph-60mph were expected along the coast from New Jersey to Maine, beginning late Friday, and up to 80mph in and around Montauk, New York.
“The nor’easter has strengthened over the Atlantic and is expected to stay closer to the shoreline. This will bring more rain inland, but more importantly stronger winds closer to shore,” Elizabeth Danco, an AccuWeather expert meteorologist, said in a statement.
“This region has experienced soaking rains in recent weeks, making it particularly susceptible to falling trees and flooding.”
While the worst of the impacts, especially flooding and beach erosion, will occur closer to the coast, travelers were warned to expect significant flight cancellations and delays, and difficult driving conditions.
Up to 8 inches of rain were forecast for some areas of south-eastern Massachusetts, and up to 2 inches in Boston on Friday into Saturday, and the same in New York City a day later. High wind warnings were in place in Boston and neighboring areas on Friday morning.
“New York City and especially Boston need to stay weather aware this weekend, and prepare the same as you would for a tropical storm,” the Weather Channel said on its website.
It also addressed the existence of the nor’easter so early in the season. “You might think it is too early for a nor’easter, but the criteria are met more often than you would think,” the Weather Channel said.
“Most people usually think of snow and ice with nor’easters because [they] do tend to occur more in the late fall and winter.”
Extreme weather is also occurring in the Pacific, where hurricanes Nolo, Odalys and Polo were bringing varying impacts on Friday. Nolo was menacing the islands of Hawaii, and expected to be a major category 3 storm as it passes about 80 miles south of Big Island early on Saturday.
Although not forecast to make landfall, Nolo will bring “five days of torrential rain through Monday, catastrophic flooding and mudslides”, AccuWeather’s hurricane experts said.
Polo, which intensified rapidly from a tropical storm to a category 5 monster hurricane earlier this week, remained offshore of Mexico on Friday, about 250 miles south-south-west of the Jalisco coast. Its 160mph winds “are likely to cause life-threatening surf, rip currents, and coastal flooding”, in the region, the National Hurricane Center in Miami said.
The storm was forecast to curve around and make landfall somewhere in Baja California on Sunday night or Monday morning as a much-weakened hurricane. Odalys, a category 4 hurricane, was forecast to remain at sea with few to no impacts on land.
The El Niño that has contributed to 18 named storms in the Pacific basin this season has had a converse effect in the Atlantic where, for the first time since 1914, no hurricanes formed by 21 September. Both seasons run until 30 November.

articles.title_orig: ICE wasted millions of taxpayer dollars in rapid push to expand detention capacity, government watchdog finds
articles.title_zh: ICE wasted millions of taxpayer dollars in rapid push to expand detention capacity, government watchdog finds
articles.content_orig:
In a single day in January, Immigration and Customs Enforcement spent more money than it had on any other day in either of President Trump's terms, federal spending records show.
The agency advanced billions to Chicago Title Insurance in escrow to acquire detention facilities, according to a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson. Over the next two months, ICE used $1.07 billion of the funds to purchase 11 warehouses it planned to convert to detention megacenters, seven of which the agency now plans to sell.
The rest of the money sat with the firm for months after ICE abandoned the warehouse plan. In July and August, ICE moved $2.2 billion from Chicago Title to purchase four detention facilities from CoreCivic, a private prison company it separately pays to continue operating them.
In its rush to expand detention capacity, ICE wasted millions of taxpayer dollars, the Government Accountability Office found in a report released Thursday. The agency failed to account for long-term costs in acquiring detention centers and lost $20 million in unrecoverable costs purchasing the warehouses it no longer plans to use, the review found. Even more could be lost if ICE sells the warehouses for less than what it paid for them, the GAO report said.
Barring any undisclosed purchases, $1.55 billion still sits with Chicago Title Insurance for acquiring detention centers as ICE continues its push to double the number of detention beds in service of the president's mass deportation agenda. Just this week, ICE awarded several companies contracts that could reach a combined $10 billion to expand and construct new facilities.
GAO concluded that "urgent planning" is necessary to reduce further waste. ICE said it would produce a strategic plan by Aug. 31, 2027, a date the watchdog said wasn't soon enough.
"We just saw a real lack of planning overall," said Heather MacLeod, director of Homeland Security and Justice at GAO. "The lack of planning has really led to stops and starts which have ultimately resulted in waste."
GAO's report did not estimate a total amount potentially lost to waste, but MacLeod said another review of ICE spending is currently underway.
Flush with cash after Congress funneled $75 billion to the agency — including $45 billion to expand detention capacity — through President Trump's " One Big Beautiful Bill Act ," ICE has nearly doubled its spending this year. The agency spent $19 billion from last October to July, the most recent month for which data is available, up from $11 billion the previous full fiscal year, a CBS News analysis of federal data found.
A DHS spokesperson wrote to CBS News that ICE is "working at turbo speed on cost-effective and innovative ways to deliver on the American people's mandate for mass deportations of criminal illegal aliens," and that the spending bill known as OBBBA has provided "historic funding" to help it carry out the mandate.
Appropriating funds outside of the typical process — and without the usual guardrails that come in appropriations bills — means ICE has more flexibility in how it can use the funding, said Kevin McNellis, a policy and budget analyst who previously worked in the Congressional Budget Office and Congressional Research Service. That also leads to a breakdown in oversight, he wrote in a report he authored for Co-Equal, a nonprofit focused on congressional authority.
"When DHS only had annual funding or relied on the annual appropriations for the majority of its funding, there were long standing systems and processes in place for DHS to inform Congress of its spending plan and for Congress to then oversee those spending plans," McNellis told CBS News. "The situation we've been in since OBBBA passed is we have an unprecedented amount of money, appropriated outside those long-standing processes, trying to be spent very quickly."
ICE paid an 11% to 13% premium on the 11 warehouses it purchased, according to CoStar, a real estate analytics firm. Former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem directed ICE to purchase new detention sites within 30 days, contributing to the high prices, The Wall Street Journal reported .
The remaining warehouses ICE still hopes to convert face legal challenges, though ICE already signed contracts worth a combined $426 million to renovate two of them. No detainees are currently held in any of the warehouses.
After dropping the warehouse plan, ICE spent $1.47 billion purchasing two California detention facilities from CoreCivic in July. The next month, ICE bought another two CoreCivic facilities in Kansas and Minnesota for a combined $734 million. In its announcement of the August purchases, CoreCivic said the company is in talks with ICE to sell more facilities.
CoreCivic is using the profits from the sales to pay down its debts, according to company filings .
GAO found that ICE had only forecasted costs for these centers and to-be-converted warehouses for the next three years, failing to consider how it would pay for them once the funds Congress has allocated through 2029 run out.
The watchdog also found that through FEMA reimbursements, ICE paid the state of Florida almost triple its typical per-bed rate for two state-operated facilities, including the now-shuttered facility dubbed "Alligator Alcatraz." ICE skipped typical contract negotiation practices, creating a new grant program with the state of Florida as the only eligible recipient, according to the GAO report. FEMA paid Florida a total of $608.4 million for "Alligator Alcatraz," GAO said.
ICE is also paying more than it typically would per-bed to house noncitizen detainees at facilities operated by the Bureau of Prisons. BOP officials told GAO they've had to pay staff overtime and for temporary assignments to meet ICE's needs, resulting in a per-bed-rate double that of ICE's median rate.
Another abandoned initiative GAO cited was ICE's efforts to launch detention facilities at military bases, like the one at Camp East Montana in El Paso. A previous GAO review found ICE spent $7.1 million on detainee meals it did not need at the El Paso facility. ICE dropped its plan to launch similar facilities on military installations in Indiana and New Jersey, GAO reported.
ICE also spent $2.85 million on tents at Guantanamo Bay to house detainees that were never used. The facility, initially planned for 30,000 detainees, held only a handful. In May, CBS News reported that the Guantanamo Bay facility was holding just six detainees. The agency is still trying to house detainees on the naval base: this week it signed a contract with the same company it used to help procure the warehouses and acquire the CoreCivic facilities to construct a facility at Guantanamo Bay and at other sites.
DHS's Inspector General is conducting its own audit into ICE's acquisition of detention space to determine whether it made purchases in a "cost-effective manner." The internal watchdog is also probing ICE spending on air charter services and its reporting on how it is using Big Beautiful Bill funds.
"We think it's important that DHS and ICE do develop a plan going forward tied to their needs and what they're trying to get out of their expansion efforts," said MacLeod, the GAO director. "We're encouraged to see that they agreed with our recommendation and we're hoping they'll take steps to address it quickly."
Sophia  Vlahakis contributed to this report.

articles.title_zh: Trump and Xi dined with AI's biggest names. Here's what we know about tech talks so far
articles.content_orig:
This report is from this week's The Tech Download newsletter. Like what you see? You can subscribe here.
It's the morning after the night before, as the U.S. President Donald Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping in a historic state dinner. Fricassée, sea bass and crémeux were all on the menu, as presumably, was a whole lot of chatter about AI.
Seated with the U.S. and Chinese presidential couples were Nvidia's Jensen Huang and his wife Lori Huang, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and AMD's Lisa Su, as well as Apple's Tim Cook. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and president Greg Brockman, Google cofounder Sergey Brin and Microsoft boss Satya Nadella were also all on the guest list.
Warnings around the existential risks of AI reaching fever pitch in recent weeks have pushed AI to the top of the global geopolitical agenda.
Trump posted to Truth Social ahead of his and Xi's head-to-head.
"Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China's position also," he wrote Thursday morning, using the term he recently adopted instead of AI.
So what did they actually discuss?
A Chinese readout of the meeting said President Xi pointed out that China and the U.S. "may have competition, but they may cooperate even more " in AI.
"The two sides can continue their dialogue on AI, exchange views on its risks and benefits, and jointly prevent the misuse and abuse of AI," Xi said, per the readout. "AI must be kept under human control. A people-centered approach should be upheld, and AI should be developed for the positive and for good, so that AI will serve the progress of humanity."
Trump, the Chinese readout stated, said the two sides should "maintain dialogue and strengthen cooperation on AI." The U.S. government had not issued its own readout of the summit as we went live.
Those references to cooperation come after U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent discussed a "U.S.-China AI dialogue" with his Chinese counterpart, He Lifeng, over the weekend, including a channel for incidents "up to a national security level."
That has been compared to the Cold War era "red phone" — a direct channel between the U.S. and Russia designed to prevent a nuclear crisis escalating.
Both U.S. and Chinese administrations had already shot down the idea of guardrails or a slowdown in developing the tech, which Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei had called for, alongside a number of their companies' researchers.
While more details about the meeting are expected to be released in the days to come, specifics are scant so far.
"It appears we ended up with an intent to continue dialogue, along with a hotline of some sort for emergencies," Aalok Mehta, director of the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told CNBC.
While the China camp's post-meeting readout sounds friendly, there were a number of flashpoints that could've made for a tense conversation.
U.S. export controls that restrict China's ability to import advanced Nvidia chips were set to remain a sticking point.
Though, as CNBC reported on Wednesday, recent new chip releases and AI models from Chinese tech giants sharpen Beijing's case that Washington's restrictions have their limits.
Friction could also have come from Chinese companies' reported remote access to Nvidia chips, via overseas data centers, and American claims of "distillation."
Time will tell if any progress was made on those issues. And if it was, there's no guarantee if either side will reveal any specific commitments.
But ongoing discussions could lead to agreements around AI with more substance, said Mehta.
"The hotline itself could become a robust tool when paired with a proper incident reporting system. But that will take real commitment to making it work and high-level engagement from both sides."
An OpenAI agent gained unauthorized access to an Australian government website, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said , raising fresh questions about the risks posed by increasingly autonomous systems.
Anthropic and OpenAI on Tuesday each announced new, less costly AI models as both frontier labs continue to face stiff competition from cheaper, open-weight competitors.
AMD stock surged 10% on Monday, pushing shares to a record high and topping a $1 trillion market cap benchmark for the first time.
Qualcomm unveiled its newest Android phone chipsets, which will be tuned for on-device AI and will compete with Apple's A20 Pro in iPhones.
OpenAI on Monday posted a set of proposals for AI safety with a heavy focus on alignment research and a computing technique known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI.
And lastly, we leave you with a hot take from an esteemed colleague. Senior tech correspondent Arjun Kharpal had this to say on Meta's Muse agent:
Meta's Muse is more of a challenge to Google than OpenAI and Anthropic.
The consumer AI market is still up for grabs and the biggest players are going to be those that can produce a useful agent, the type that companies have promised. Plus, they'll need to earn the trust of users, especially as we have had all of these cybersecurity incidents recently.
Google has all the ingredients to have done this first — control of a mobile operating system in Android, search dominance, a plethora of apps from email to maps. All of that should have allowed it to create a useful agent with Gemini that could potentially be powerful on Android devices, which make up the majority of the world's smartphones.
But Meta has beaten it to the punch.
That's not to say Google is down and out, but Meta has certainly laid down the gauntlet. To some extent, Meta is also challenging Apple to come up with something strong with Siri to ensure the Cupertino giant can leverage its massive install base of iOS users.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo XIV begins historic 4-day visit to France
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo XIV begins historic 4-day visit to France
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo arrived in France on Friday, Sept. 25, starting a four-day tour across Paris, Lourdes, and Metz that includes speeches and a massive outdoor mass. (HOST BROADCASTER via Reuters.)
Pope Leo XIV began his visit to France on Friday for his fifth Apostolic Journey as Pontiff. The four-day trip marks the first formal papal visit to the country once called "the eldest daughter of the Church" since Pope Benedict XVI’s visit in September 2008.
French bishops announced the visit’s theme as "That the world may have life," and it comes as the officially secular nation is seeing an influx of new baptisms. So far this year, according to the Conference of Bishops of France, more than 21,000 adults have joined the Church, an increase driven by 18 to 25-year-olds.
"Pope Leo's visit to France has sparked a real tidal wave" of interest, retired French Bishop Marc Stenger told Reuters. "French Catholics are… saying ​loudly that they need the Church to find their way in these uncertain moments in world history."
POPE LEO WARNS AI RISKS BECOMING TOOL OF 'DOMINATION, EXCLUSION AND DEATH' IN NEW ENCYCLICAL
The pope will visit Metz on Sept. 28, 2026 to conclude his four-day state and pastoral trip to France, which also includes stops in Paris and Lourdes. (Jean-Christophe Verhaegen / AFP via Getty Images)
The rise comes after a 2021 report found that some 330,000 French children had been abused by Catholic clergy and lay leaders over seven decades, and said the Church had shown "deep, total and even cruel indifference" ​to victims. Stenger, who led the Diocese of Troyes from 1999 to 2020, told Reuters the scandals "have deeply wounded the Church and damaged its credibility."
In what is described as an unusual move, the Vatican press office announced Pope Leo will meet privately in Lourdes with seven of those victims as part of a message of healing and vulnerability.
SAN FRANCISCO ARCHDIOCESE AGREES TO $395M SETTLEMENT WITH 530 CLERGY ABUSE SURVIVORS
The Vatican calls the trip, "a journey that unites faith and public engagement, memory and the future, with listening and bridge-building at its heart." After being greeted by French President Emmanuel Macron and a courtesy visit to Élysée Palace on Friday, Pope Leo is scheduled to make 15 speeches during his visit. He is expected to speak on several spiritual and societal themes, including the need to protect immigrants , the sick and unborn, and defend human dignity in the era of AI, and address themes of peace, culture, and unity.
President of France Emmanuel Macron and First Lady Brigitte Macron welcome Pope Leo XIV to Élysée Palace on Sept. 25, 2026 in Paris, France. (Tom Nicholson/Getty Images)
French bishops have expressed surprise at the level of interest in the visit. The Associated Press reports organizers for Pope Leo’s Saturday Mass at Paris’ Place de la Concorde, expecting up to 1 million people, have lengthened the security perimeter, extending the site beyond the 1.2-mile length of the Champs-Élysées, where Pope Leo will parade in the Popemobile.
Among his more noteworthy stops, Pope Leo will worship and speak on Sunday at the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, one of Christianity’s most-visited pilgrimage destinations, especially popular with the sick. It is where an ailing Pope John Paul II , on his final foreign trip in 2004, delivered a forceful condemnation of abortion and euthanasia.
Pope Leo XIV attends the Welcome Ceremony at Paris Orly International Airport on Sept. 25, 2026 in Paris, France. (Simone Risoluti - Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images)
Pope Leo’s visit, however, comes after France’s recent national debate and subsequent passage of legislation allowing adults with incurable illnesses to receive lethal medication. That followed 2024 legislation enshrining abortion as a constitutional right .
POPE LEO PROMOTES ARCHBISHOP WHO BARRED PELOSI FROM COMMUNION TO ONE OF VATICAN'S HIGHEST COURTS
On Friday, Pope Leo will speak at the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, or UNESCO, headquarters in Paris. Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni says Leo will likely reiterate his call for an AI slowdown and speak "with regard to the meaning of existence, to what makes human beings human and what does not."
The speech comes after the Pope’s May manifesto in which Leo warned of the dangers of AI and urged international regulation of the industry. His position again puts him at odds with President Trump, who has encouraged AI innovation so the U.S. can compete with and surpass China.
A crucifix stands in front of the Basilique Notre-Dame du Rosaire, its spire draped with a banner marking the upcoming visit of Pope Leo XIV, five days ahead of the pontiff's trip to the site as part of his apostolic journey to France, in Lourdes on Sept. 22, 2026.
Following his UNESCO visit, Pope Leo holds a prayer service at the newly-restored Cathedral of Notre-Dame, marking the first papal visit since a 2019 fire nearly destroyed one of France’s national landmarks.
He concludes his trip on Monday with a symbolic full-day visit to the border city of Metz, the birthplace of former French Prime Minister Robert Schuman, considered one of the founding fathers of the European Union. It is a backdrop the Vatican says the Pope will use to "champion friendship among European peoples."

French Ambassador to the Vatican Charles Personnaz told Reuters that Macron has invited leaders from all 27 EU members to attend the speech and meet with the Pontiff. Other media reports say Ukrainian President V olodymyr Zelenskyy may also attend.
Reuters and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: With Republicans under pressure, Trump’s White House starts bending
articles.title_zh: With Republicans under pressure, Trump’s White House starts bending
articles.content_orig:
Seen on a screen below an exit sign, President Trump speaks on the first day of the 2026 Republican convention on Sept. 9 in Dallas. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images hide caption
There's a rare thing happening inside President Trump's Republican Party: dissent.
The president has long insisted on loyalty, but in recent weeks, a growing number of Republican candidates and elected officials have distanced themselves from core pieces of his agenda: from calling for an end to the U.S. war with Iran and relief from high prices, to criticizing his handling of key agenda issues like immigration.
It comes at a critical moment for the GOP. With less than 40 days until voting ends, the party is scrambling to hold onto a slim majority in Congress, where control of both the Senate and House of Representatives could come down to just a handful of toss-up races.
Trump's presence in the midterms looms large. He has repeatedly told voters to vote like he is on the ballot , despite facing historically low approval ratings . That could backfire, according to the latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll , which finds that a plurality of registered voters, 45%, and a majority of independents, view their vote as a vote against Trump.
"Trump's strength has always been primarily devised from his relationship to the voters," said Sarah Longwell, a GOP strategist and longtime critic of the president. "Republicans have always been loath to cross him because of his sort of stronghold on the party."
However, as Americans continue to sour on the president, Longwell argued that GOP lawmakers and candidates alike may "feel more comfortable bucking him on things that they really care about."
While most of the Republicans who have distanced themselves are on the ballot this fall, the splits have not been solely confined to the campaign trail.
On Tuesday, Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, who isn't up for reelection until 2030, released a letter urging the Senate Judiciary Committee to investigate the president's son, Donald Trump Jr., after ProPublica reported that a Russian oligarch financed large portions of a lavish party to celebrate his wedding.
Though past Trump-critics have largely been voted out of Congress or left the party, and the president still enjoys overwhelming support from Republican voters, Longwell sees Curtis' move as a potential indicator that lawmakers view the president's coalition as increasingly fragile.
"You are starting to see the very beginnings of people recognizing that Trump just doesn't have the juice that he once did and starting to push back."
In poll after poll, Americans consistently rank the cost of living as their top concern, and now, many say the conflict has added additional financial strain on their lives.
It's a connection that some Republican candidates running in toss-up races this cycle are acknowledging. On Monday, two GOP Senate candidates – Ashley Hinson of Iowa and Mike Rogers of Michigan – came out against the war and lobbied for additional relief for Americans impacted by rising costs.
"Iowans are being squeezed and shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran," Hinson said in a statement on X , adding the conflict "needs to be brought to a successful and immediate end."
The comments marked a shift for Hinson, who has previously voted against efforts to end the war .
In a video filmed at a supermarket, Rogers also made a point to link rising prices to the conflict.
"Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life. Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down. The war with Iran needs to end and end quickly. When it does, energy costs will plummet," he said.
Neither Hinson nor Rogers directly mentioned Trump in their statements, but their comments marked a clear break with the White House, given Trump has consistently defended his decision to go to war with Iran and has downplayed the conflict's effect on the economy.
There appears to be growing impatience with the war on Capitol Hill too. Just last week, seven House Republican lawmakers — up from four over the summer — joined Democrats in supporting a resolution aiming to remove U.S. forces from Iran.
"For a long time, Republicans have stuck with the president through thick and thin. But the ones who are facing real trouble at the polls need to differentiate themselves," said Ron Bonjean, a GOP strategist and founder of the public affairs firm ROKK Solutions.
By choosing to cross Trump this late in the election cycle, Bonjean said it underscores how high the stakes are for Republicans.
"They're doing everything they can to make sure voters understand that they're much more independent than voting with Trump 100% or agreeing with him 100% of the time," he added.
That independence could prove crucial for Republicans whose political fate may be determined by some of the same key voting blocs that moved right two years ago and have since distanced from Trump, namely, Hispanic voters.
Even in red states like Texas and Florida, House districts with large Hispanic populations have seen drops in Republican support, according to a recent New York Times/Siena poll .
That includes Florida's 27th district, where Rep. María Elvira Salazar is running to represent parts of Miami for a third term.
Last week, she released an ad directly criticizing Trump's immigration agenda, arguing his enforcement efforts have "gone too far."
"Be careful what your advisers are telling you about immigration policy," said Salazar, whose district is rated by the Cook Political Report as likely Republican. "The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today."
Like many Republicans, Salazar is still walking a fine line. In an interview with CBS News days after releasing her ad, she acknowledged having a "fantastic conversation," with Trump and described him as "very receptive."
"There are no attacks here," she added. "I'm just forewarning him and advising him as a member of Congress from the South Florida area that some of his advisers are just not presenting the whole picture."

articles.title_orig: US backs Elon Musk's bid to overturn €120m EU fine against X
articles.title_zh: US backs Elon Musk's bid to overturn €120m EU fine against X
articles.content_orig:
The US government is seeking to join Elon Musk's legal challenge to overturn a €120m (£105m) EU fine against X over its blue tick badges.
In December 2025, the European Commission said the platform "deceives users" by allowing people to pay for a blue verified check mark, because it is not "meaningfully verifying" who is behind the account.
But US Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate said on Thursday that the commission had "inappropriately attempted" to expand its reach to American companies outside its control.
Musk, who spent millions helping elect Donald Trump and other Republicans, has previously claimed EU tech regulation "inhibits progress" for companies.
The US Department of Justice (DOJ) has filed an application with the EU's General Court in support of Musk's and X's attempts to dismiss ​the case.
It claims that under a section of law in the Statute of the Court of Justice of the EU, a state may intervene in disputes before the court if it "can establish an interest in the result of the case to the court".
The DOJ said the US "has a clear interest" in ensuring any decision by the commission was applied consistently with "how territorial jurisdiction is generally understood in international law".
It also wants to make sure it would not "otherwise prejudice" US-headquartered digital services that "contribute significantly" to its economy.
In a press briefing on Friday , European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier said it was "ready to defend" its position in court.
He added that the commission had an "solid case" at its disposal, due to the alleged breach of its Digital Services Act.
In addition to its use of blue ticks, EU regulators had accused X of failing to provide transparency around its adverts and denying researchers access to public data.
Henna Virkkunen, the regulator's executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, said at the time of the fine's issue it was "holding X responsible for undermining users' rights and evading accountability".
"Deceiving users with blue checkmarks, obscuring information on ads and shutting out researchers have no place online in the EU," she said.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) had criticised the EU regulator, accusing it of attacking and censoring US firms.
"The European Commission's fine isn't just an attack on X, it's an attack on all American tech platforms and the American people by foreign governments," Rubio wrote in a post on X.
"The days of censoring Americans online are over."
His remarks were reposted by Musk, who added "absolutely".
The European Commission denied targeting any specific nationality, stating it is simply protecting its digital and democratic standards to maintain its role as a global benchmark.
The action marked the Commission's first official non-compliance decision under the Digital Services Act (DSA), one of two mandatory rulebooks governing online platforms in the EU.
However, the EU is also conducting several other investigations into the platform, including one into its integrated AI assistant Grok over concerns it was used to create sexualised images of real people.

This year’s New York Film Festival is bursting with some of the best and buzziest offerings in the 64-year-old festival’s recent history. World premieres include new films by Luca Guadagnino (“Artificial”), Tom McCarthy (“A Statement”), Ava DuVernay (“14th”), and Tony Gilroy (“Behemoth!”). NYFF audiences will also be the first to catch movies like James Gray’s opening nighter “Paper Tiger” (a North American premiere) and Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes doc “You Can See Everything” fresh from their respective Cannes and Telluride bows.
The film ‘s international spectrum boasts a range of world premieres as well, from the Iranian documentary “ I Deserve a Lover Whose Every Rise Sets Fiery Dooms Raging Across the Skies ” to debate-stoking Mexican art filmmaker Carlos Reygadas’ authoritarianism sci-fi “Heil Jupiter!,” his first film in eight years. The NYFF once again promises a sophisticated event tailored to both highbrow cinephiles looking for a challenge (the five-and-change-hour documentary “Life of Jorge Luis Borges,” anyone?) and the more crowd-pleaser-inclined (like two A24 pictures, Chris Rock’s “Misty Green” and Jordan Firstman’s Cannes smash “Club Kid”).
“I do think that that’s what we think about, especially programming a festival for a city like New York, is to think about multiple potential audiences,” said NYFF artistic director Dennis Lim, whose programming team scouts film festivals big and small, year to year, looking to outfit its various noncompetitive sections. This year, the festival is showing 113 films, and from filmmakers like Jesse Eisenberg, Mike Leigh, Radu Jude, Lee Chang-dong, Eleanor Coppola, Werner Herzog, Pawel Pawlikowski, Pedro Almodóvar, and even Ken Russell, with a 35mm print of his recently restored, heretical 1971 shocker “The Devils.”
Takashi Yamazaki’s “Godzilla Minus Zero” also marks its world premiere at NYFF this weekend, a rare blockbuster bow for the festival. Releasing through its subsidiary GKIDS in the U.S., the Toho epic first-looks in New York even before its hometown Tokyo Film Festival screening. “Godzilla’s” positioning at NYFF feels closely linked to the premiere of Na Hong-jin’s VFX-heavy monster movie “Hope” in the Cannes competition. As more studios cower from showing their high-profile films at festivals to avoid terrible early reviews (possibly hence no “Digger” out of Venice from Warners), international tentpoles can fill the void.
“I think we create a great context for a film,” Lim said. “It’s New York, so there’s just a certain critical mass of press and industry, and I think people have a certain trust that the film is going to be received by a sophisticated cine-literate audience.” Meaning that just because it’s Godzilla doesn’t mean it won’t have the imprimatur of art .
When Guadagnino’s Sam Altman dramedy “Artificial,” said to be a biting critique of AI’s takeover of our planet, hot-potatoed from tech giant Amazon to much indier outfit Neon for predictable reasons, Lim and his team moved quickly. Most of the Italian director’s movies have screened here in New York, including the divisive “After the Hunt,” which opened last year’s festival ahead of the annual Tavern on the Green fete.
“Even though everybody knew about this film and knew it was completed, the situation with the studios was played out in public,” Lim said of the Andrew Garfield starrer. “We didn’t know whether this would even be a film for this year until fairly late in the process. Once it landed with Neon, we started having that conversation, and I saw it not long after Neon picked it up and was immediately convinced that this is a film that we should show and we should get behind.”
Lim said that Guadagnino, who just received a career prize at the Venice Film Festival where he premiered his seven-hour Bertolucci nonfiction deep dive “ Joie de Vivre ,” is “the kind of filmmaker who just never stays still. He’s always moving from one kind of film to another. I think this film, it’s gotten even more scarily topical since I saw it in July. I mean, if you look at the news this week, everything that’s happened in the AI space in the last two months…”
NYFF is also the first and most urgent stop domestically for the harrowing, must-see documentary “ NAZA ,” from the Israeli half of the Oscar-winning “No Other Land” collective, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor. The Guardian Films-produced documentary, which features interviews with IDF members about the inner workings of the war on Gaza, is being rushed into theatrical self-release at IFC Center mere days after its September 26, sold-out NYFF premiere. The stakes are high, as Israeli officials campaign against Abraham and Szor’s citizenship status, and atrocity in Gaza wages on. At the film’s press screening earlier this month, journalists had to submit their laptops and cellphones to festival PR to avoid leaks; IndieWire confirmed that won’t be the case for ticketed festivalgoers.
A completely different movie also demanded discretion: the Telluride smash “You Can See Everything.” “The plan all along was to keep that film [under wraps]. Even the existence of the film was supposed to be a secret, which was also the case with ‘NAZA,’ a very different film where confidentiality was needed for very different reasons,” Lim said.
Unlike many of its fall festival predecessors (including TIFF proper for the first time this year), NYFF doesn’t have a market per se. But it is an opportunity to put your movie in front of New York film industry players if it’s still seeking a buyer. Like Ira Sachs’ “The Man I Love,” an AIDS-era love triangle set in 1980s New York City and starring Rami Malek and Tom Sturridge. The “Passages” director, a longtime favorite of the New York Film Festival and a fixture of the NYC film scene, premiered the film to supportive reviews in the Cannes competition this past May. The drama still does not have domestic distribution despite playing Karlovy Vary and Telluride post-Cannes. Gay narratives are always a challenge for buyers, especially around AIDS, and the Andrew Scott Oscar-hopeful “Elsinore” is occupying a sizable chunk of that space right now. As is “La Bola Negra.” But NYFF will help platform “The Man I Love” to what should be an appreciative New York (and queer) audience.
“Obviously, we don’t have a formal market, but being in New York where a lot of the players are based, there’s certainly industry activity at the festival, industry presence,” Lim said. “We typically find that most films that are in the Main Slate end up with distribution of some form, even if it’s a smaller film with a smaller distributor. And I think Ira’s film is one of the most striking and one of the boldest American films of the year. I have no doubt he’ll get picked up. And if we can play some small part in that, I’m thrilled.”
As for nabbing “Paper Tiger’s” North American premiere ahead of Neon’s November release, Lim said those conversations started “very early” with James Gray, in the spring before Cannes.
“We were lucky to see that film early,” Lim said. “James is a filmmaker who means a lot to me, and who also has had a long relationship with us at the festival. And I think that this is like a pinnacle for him. I think it’s a remarkable film. I think it’s very difficult to make films like this today. This is a film that is unapologetically sincere. It’s like a classical film. It’s not gimmicky. It’s a James Gray film. It’s a New York film. And I think for us, we have the right audience to really appreciate what he’s accomplished with this film. I think it’s an incredible achievement, and we’re very proud to be opening with this film. I think it’s career-best, or close to career-best,

articles.title_orig: Michigan GOP Senate candidate who praised the Iran war now campaigns against the pain it caused
articles.title_zh: Michigan GOP Senate candidate who praised the Iran war now campaigns against the pain it caused
articles.content_orig:
In 2024, then-Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers stood on camera in a zippered vest in a large grocery store.
“This is your grocery cart under a Trump economy,” Rogers said in the 13-second video , pointing to a normal-sized grocery cart. Rogers then pulled out a toddler-sized cart next to it: “This is your grocery cart under a Biden-Harris economy. Take note, in November.”
Two years later, Rogers is again running for Senate in Michigan as a Republican, and again running ads from grocery stores. Clad in a near identical outfit, in what appears to be the same grocery store chain, Rogers opens a new campaign ad by saying bluntly, “Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down.”
But this time, rather than calling out an unpopular presidential administration, Rogers blames the war with Iran for soaring prices.
“The war with Iran needs to end and end quickly,” Rogers says. “When it does, energy costs will plummet, but Michigan families can’t afford to wait for that to happen.”
The ad underscores the trouble Republicans face as they campaign to fix the affordability crisis worsened by the war. It also marks a notable shift in tone for Rogers, who has consistently supported President Donald Trump’s decision to attack Iran and whose national security background and hawkish foreign policy views have long been a central part of his political identity.
In the weeks and months after the war began on February 28, Rogers spoke in favor of Trump’s decision and called the war “ long overdue .” In April, he said the war had left Iran “ absolutely a toothless wonder” and called it “the best opportunity for peace in the Middle East I think I’ve ever seen in my lifetime” during an appearance on CNN contributor Scott Jennings’ radio show.
And in continued interviews on conservative talk radio in March through July, Rogers consistently defended the war and argued the United States should continue its effort against Iran, according to a CNN KFile review of his statements.
Rogers’s new ad comes just six weeks before he faces Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who has strongly condemned the war. Recent polling also indicates the war has become deeply unpopular with Americans. A new CNN poll conducted by SSRS found that nearly two-thirds of respondents said the US is not winning the conflict, and more than three-quarters said the war is not worth it.
For Rogers, the unpopular war presents one of the biggest challenges to his now years-long effort to win a US Senate seat in Michigan. Rogers first launched a campaign for Senate in September 2023, ultimately losing to Democrat Elissa Slotkin in November 2024.
Five months later, in April 2025, Rogers launched a second bid for Senate, this time to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters.
Rogers ran unopposed for the Republican nomination and has spent much of the general election portraying El-Sayed, a former Detroit public health director, as outside Michigan’s political mainstream. He has pointed to El-Sayed’s association with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker and progressive comments that El-Sayed scrubbed from the internet before launching his campaign.
A spokesperson for the campaign pointed to comments Rogers made at a press conference addressing his ad calling to end the war with Iran.
“We’ve been pretty patient on the timeline,” Rogers said on Wednesday. “I think the best option now is to wind it down. There’s still other things you can do to make sure that they can’t hurt their neighbors and can’t pursue a nuclear weapon.”
Noting the rising price of diesel, Rogers said it would take a “horrific toll” on farmers during harvest season and grocery prices. “You just can’t let it go and linger. Now’s the time to start winding this thing up,” he said, referring to the war with Iran.
As a Republican congressman for more than a decade beginning in the early 2000s, Rogers was a staunch supporter of America’s global war on terror launched in the wake of the 9/11 attacks, eventually chairing the House Intelligence Committee. Rogers was quick to come out in support of Trump’s decision to attack Iran in February.
He publicly backed the military action on the day it began, calling Iran an “imminent threat to our country” that “must not have a nuclear weapon” in a post on X.
A month later on a podcast from March, Rogers argued Americans should unite behind the military operation against Iran and “get it done right” before debating whether the intervention was wise.
“People say, well, ‘what date is it going to end?’ It shouldn’t be a date. It should be conditional,” Rogers said on the Joe Pags Show podcast. “When can they no longer mine the Straits of Hormuz? When can they no longer send drones into the side of commercial ships, which they have been doing, threatened to do and did before? …This is why Americans need to stop for a minute, come together and say, ‘let’s get this done, get it done right.’”
By April, Rogers suggested the war would be over soon.
“We’re not going to do this forever. I think this is the right thing to do. I do think it will be over quickly because the military piece of this, they’re getting down to the last targets,” he said on The Clay Travis and Buck Sexton Show in April.
In May, Rogers acknowledged the war’s economic costs, saying on a conservative podcast that the “Iran issue has caused gas prices go up” and that “hurts everybody.” But he also maintained his support for the war’s rationale, saying, “I also support the fact that Iran should not have a nuclear weapon.”
In July, Rogers emphasized that he wanted the war to wrap up, telling the Fox News Rundown podcast, “I want it over as fast as possible. I want the president to do the kind of actions he needs to do to get it done as soon as possible so we can get those prices coming back down.”
By the end of that month, however, Rogers said that he supported giving Trump more time on the war to finish negotiations: “I don’t mind giving the president authority to continue. You can’t stop in mid-negotiation. I think that would not be good for America,” Rogers told CBS Detroit in a TV interview. “But I want him to wrap it up. And my understanding is he’s doing just that.”

articles.title_zh: Here are the lyrics to the 4 new Taylor Swift songs off 'The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore'
articles.content_orig:
(Republic) This four-track addition to a critically maligned album works hard to remind fans what they love about Swift, with some sweet highs and galling lows
O ne downside of turning your release strategies into scavenger hunts and layering clues within your work is that it invites enormous amounts of scrutiny about your potential motive. When Taylor Swift announced an expanded edition of last year’s critically maligned The Life of a Showgirl this week, subtitled The Encore, many fans instantly suspected one of two things: that it was designed to remind Grammy members of Showgirl’s existence during their voting period to determine next year’s nominees, or to oust country ingenue Ella Langley from her record-breaking US No 1 run .
If that sounds cynical, it’s also worth remembering that when Swift announced Showgirl last year, she said that unlike her previous album, The Tortured Poets Department – a 16-track record immediately inflated to 31 songs on release day – the purposefully concise, 12-track Showgirl would not be expanded. (This didn’t stop her releasing 34 variants of the record, with various acoustic demos and so on, to juice sales.)
After Showgirl had the biggest US opening week ever, Swift went to Sweden to celebrate with collaborators Max Martin and Shellback, she revealed this week. The trip was intended to be about reflection and gratitude, she wrote on Instagram. “But,” she continued, “there was a studio there and we did what we do when we feel anything at all: we wrote more songs.” One hesitates to liken Swift to Kanye West, but The Life of a Showgirl is starting to look a little more like The Life of Pablo , West’s endlessly extended seventh album.
A slipperiness has infected the whole endeavour, not helped by Swift’s initial promise that Showgirl was all “bangers” and about “keeping the bar really high”, a claim quickly dismissed: the record is a travesty, a word that feels particularly apt when you recall Wood , a Bruno Mars-lite abomination about her now-husband Travis Kelce’s penis. And for an album that was supposed to be about the giddy highs of life on Swift’s own record-breaking Eras tour, it contained a tedious amount of well-worn score-settling . Adding four more songs written some time after the initial sessions further dilutes the record’s already flimsy premise.
The most Swiftian thing about these four tracks is their visceral sense of course-correction. For all that Swift chafes against The Haters – more on them to come, shocker – she’s always reacting to criticism. Recall the scene from her Miss Americana documentary where she learns that her sixth album, Reputation , didn’t get nominated for the album of the year Grammy: “I just need to make a better record,” she says, visibly crushed. (That’s the folly of working like this: Reputation is her best record, and those voters are idiots.) Showgirl was panned for its excessive wordiness and defaulting on the promised bangers; these Encore songs largely pare back the verbiage and double down on hooks and firework-laden bridges, Swift’s metier. It’s like watching an ambitious chorus line dancer breathlessly flay herself in the spotlight to prove herself worthy of our love.
Every Swift album except Reputation has a deluxe version, though just a handful of those bonus songs are keepers: Jump Then Fall (from Fearless), New Romantics (1989), Bigger Than the Whole Sky and Would’ve Could’ve Should’ve (Midnights). None of these new songs are destined to join those ranks, though Patient Zero comes closest. Hooked around a mournful and curiously processed Celtic fiddle sample, it recalls the spirit of Lover , where it felt as though Swift was trying out potential new sonic futures. Its pained chorus also evokes Tortured Poets’ Fortnight : a slinky, low-key yet insidiously catchy melodic Möbius strip, with lyrics offering connection to a woman recently burned by an ex whose games Swift knows well.
It’s one of two Encore songs that contain a palpable sense of humanity, unlike anything from its childish parent album. Pink Clouding is a mature apology to a kind ex she let down – “Neither of us knew at the time / That I was a liar” – filled with the sort of regret that will never lose its shameful sting. Unlike Swift’s post-2020 turn to heavily detailed narrative writing, it’s written in a pure-pop form, braiding shades of pink and various flowers into a sweet and effective conceit without defaulting on emotional grace. It is ardent synth-pop, a sweet balance of airy and punchy; it also sounds a little like it could’ve lived next to Cruel Summer on Lover, though truthfully it recalls Tegan and Sara’s classic 2013 album Heartthrob, which inspired Swift’s 1989 pop makeover.
The beauty of Pink Clouding is that it sounds genuinely believable, a quality curiously missing from Swift’s songs about Kelce. Tortured Poets bonus track So High School is as close as she’s gotten; the Showgirl songs about their romance framed it as a triumph over venal and conniving haters. It’s a very strange lens through which to write about supposed true love, and one she returns to here. The appalling Cleveland! is all about how Kelce loves her despite internet commenters saying she can’t dance (a long-dead criticism) and that she’s annoying, and is sung with such oozing self-satisfaction it’s like being repeatedly poked and asked if it hurts. Spiritually, it is a cut-and-shut of two of her worst songs ever, Lover’s Me! (about being cringe but free) and Showgirl’s Honey (about other women being jealous haters). Despite her long-term collaborator Jack Antonoff not being part of the Showgirl era, it still sounds like warmed-over Bleachers.
after newsletter promotion
It is a mess of contradictions: it has an oddly sour tang for such a festive, all-bells-jangling confection, like biting into a lavishly iced cake to find the sugar swapped for salt. For a song about having found the one, its standards are barrel-scrapingly low: “You only need to find one person in this entire world / Who doesn’t find you completely insufferable!” she declares. Girl! Aim higher! Where on Honey, and other recent songs, she has proven strikingly eager to call other women bitches, here she coyly stops short of calling herself a “whore” and “bitch” in incomplete lines that make conspicuous features of those gaps.
And for all that she laments the haters, she sure does write a lot of songs about them. The more dogshit like Cleveland! she releases, the more criticism it may garner, in turn generating inspiration for … more songs like this. It is Swiftian Groundhog Day: she seems unwilling or unable to extricate herself from the vast web of self-reference she now seems condemned to operate within, having reached the point in the corporate life cycle where novelty is all but exhausted and it’s easier to double down on core values.
It’s hard to tell what any of this has to do with Showgirl (other than pushing the album back to No 1 until Christmas). Every song sounds as though it could have been appended to a different record. Closing track Babylon is sub- Evermore in its overcomplicated narrative of a fractured family and grave, watery production. You could point to their very loose shared theme, each taking different angles on the gap between a facade and an intimately understood truth – though the greater truth affirmed by this batch of music is that the more Swift releases, the weaker her output gets. It doesn’t take any detective work to deduce that the healthiest thing for her creativity would be to let the curtain fall for a while.

articles.title_orig: Russia could attack a NATO country within months, Danish intelligence warns

articles.content_orig:
Danish intelligence officials have warned that Russia could launch a "limited" military attack against a NATO member in the coming months, saying the Kremlin appears more willing to take risks after more than 4½ years of war against Ukraine.
The Danish Defence Intelligence Service, or DDIS, on Thursday identified a "low but growing risk" that Russia could carry out isolated strikes with long-range weapons on infrastructure that is critical to the support of Ukraine.
"A limited military attack would be a desperate move on Russia's part and, like the intensified hybrid attacks, could potentially take place in the coming months," it wrote in a report.
"The purpose would be to redirect European resources away from supporting Ukraine and to sow division within NATO, should the alliance fail to agree on a collective response."
The DDIS added that it saw no indications that Russia would launch an outright invasion of a NATO country, although it said it could not rule this out.
Russia could also deploy a limited number of troops, possibly without national insignia, into NATO countries on its border, the DDIS said. However, it said that such a buildup would be difficult to conceal and take several months to prepare.
The new threat assessment joins a chorus of Russia warnings from top European security officials and lawmakers in recent days.
NATO members that border Russia are Finland, Norway and Poland as well as the Baltic states of Latvia, Estonia and Lithuania.
Poland's government on Thursday said a blaze at a Starlink ground station in the country was an act of sabotage aimed at disrupting internet services, including for Ukraine's military.
Poland's deputy prime minister, Krzysztof Gawkowski, said it had not yet been established who was responsible for the fire, but "many signs suggest this aligns with Russia's new ‌doctrine ⁠of attack," according to Reuters .
A spokesperson for Russia's embassy in London was not immediately available to comment when contacted by CNBC. The Kremlin has previously denied involvement in similar incidents.
Denmark's intelligence service also warned that Russia will intensify its hybrid war by carrying out more attacks against the West and NATO, "with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past."
These could include major cyberattacks that seriously damage vital societal functions as well as sabotage attacks with a high risk of casualties, the DDIS said.

articles.content_orig:
FILE - A campaign rally site for Republican presidential candidate former President Donald Trump is empty and littered with debris on July 13, 2024, in Butler, Pa. Evan Vucci/AP hide caption
James Copenhaver, one of three campaign rally attendees shot in 2024 during an assassination attempt on then-candidate Donald Trump, has died in Pittsburgh, his lawyer said Thursday. He was 76.
Copenhaver was in the bleachers during the event in Butler, Pennsylvania, when a 20-year-old gunman opened fire from a nearby rooftop, grazing Trump's right ear with one bullet. Copenhaver was struck in the arm and in the abdomen, wounds that left him with lingering injuries and walking with a cane.
Two other attendees were also shot — David Dutch, who survived, and Corey Comperatore, who shielded his family from gunfire and was killed.
Copenhaver died Wednesday at Allegheny Health Network's West Penn Hospital in Pittsburgh, according to a statement from the Allegheny County medical examiner cited in local media accounts.
Copenhaver's lawyer, Joseph Feldman, said in a statement issued on behalf of the family that he died surrounded by loved ones. The statement did not specify if his death was directly related to the injuries he suffered at the rally.
Copenhaver and his wife, Marianne Copenhaver, sued the federal government in June, alleging that the Secret Service and Department of Homeland Security had "utterly failed" to provide appropriate security at the rally. Copenhaver's injuries required multiple surgeries, including a transection of his colon, and he had lingering kidney and other damage, including a loss of feeling in his leg. The lawsuit described the wounds as "debilitating, grievous, permanent and life altering."
The family's statement Thursday called Copenhaver above all else a devoted husband, father and grandfather who instilled the values of hard work, integrity and the service to others in his children.
"James's dedication to this great country was a defining part of his life," it said. "As a veteran, he proudly served our nation in the armed forces, and his love of country never wavered. James was a true American patriot who believed deeply in the freedoms and ideals upon which this nation was founded, and he embodied the very best traits of our great nation."
In a statement posted to social media, Trump on Thursday called Copenhaver "a true American Patriot."
"Jim showed tremendous bravery, courageously continuing to FIGHT, FIGHT, FIGHT, and maintaining a positive spirit despite unimaginable hardships," Trump wrote.
