articles.title_zh: Internet and phone network disrupted in Ethiopia's war-hit Tigray region
articles.content_orig:
Nearly four years ago, a peace deal ended the brutal war in Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, one of the deadliest conflicts of the 21st century. Now, the violence has returned — but the battle lines have changed.
Tigrayan rebels are again fighting the federal government, while forces that were once enemies are now fighting side by side.
On Wednesday, Tigrayan forces seized three airports controlled by the federal government, while fighting also broke out in the neighboring regions of Amhara and Afar.
The hostilities have shattered the 2022 peace agreement that ended a war estimated to have killed around 600,000 people . Relations between the federal government and Tigray’s leaders had been worsening for months.
It’s unclear what led to the recent fighting, with both sides offering conflicting accounts.
Tigray’s regional government said federal forces attacked first and that it ordered its forces to respond, calling it a “defensive war.” While Getachew Reda, an adviser to Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, said the TPLF had launched an “all-out offensive” against government positions in Afar and Amhara and seized the three airports in Tigray, accusing it of taking “irresponsibility to new heights.”
The renewed violence this week follows almost two months of smaller clashes. The nongovernmental organization Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) says fighting between Tigrayan and federal forces began near Ethiopia’s border with Sudan on August 1. The two sides also accused each other of starting those clashes.
According to ACLED, federal drone strikes and Tigrayan troop deployments followed, with Tigrayan forces moving tanks and artillery south this month.
National carrier Ethiopian Airlines has suspended all flights to Tigray after the airport seizures.
The TPLF was once Ethiopia’s most powerful political force. It dominated the coalition that governed the country for nearly three decades, despite Tigrayans making up a relatively small share of Ethiopia’s population.
That changed after Abiy became prime minister in 2018 following years of anti-government protests. He introduced political reforms and made peace with neighboring Eritrea, which won him the Nobel Peace Prize a year later.
But relations with the TPLF deteriorated. Abiy replaced the old ruling coalition with his Prosperity Party in 2019; the TPLF refused to join.
‘Practically this has been a genocide’
After national elections were postponed during the Covid-19 pandemic, Tigray held its own regional vote despite objections from Addis Ababa.
In November 2020, Tigrayan forces attacked federal military bases in the region. Abiy sent troops in, and Eritrean forces and fighters from Amhara later fought alongside the federal army.
By the time the war ended two years later, millions of people had been displaced and parts of Tigray had been pushed into famine. Both sides faced accusations of serious human rights abuses.
Hostilities came to an end when the federal government and TPLF signed an African Union-brokered agreement in Pretoria, South Africa, on November 2, 2022.
Under the deal, Tigrayan forces were to disarm and federal authority would return to the region. Humanitarian aid and basic services would resume, and an interim administration was later set up to govern Tigray until elections.
But major disputes remained, including over territory claimed by both Tigray and Amhara and the return of people displaced by the war. Meanwhile, Eritrea, whose soldiers had fought alongside federal forces, was not party to the agreement.
“The agreement didn’t collapse overnight — it was systematically hollowed out over three years,” Surafel Getahun, an Ethiopian geopolitics researcher, told CNN.
Getahun said both sides bore responsibility. He accused the federal government of failing to fulfill key parts of the agreement, including returning displaced people, and the TPLF of breaching it by retaking control of the regional administration and rebuilding its military forces.
The TPLF was also divided by an internal power struggle , which further weakened the peace process. Rival factions emerged around TPLF chairman Debretsion Gebremichael and Reda, the head of the Tigray interim administration who had been a senior TPLF figure. Reda was later expelled from the party by Gebremichael’s faction, and Abiy appointed a new interim leader in April 2025.
A month later, Gebremichael’s faction took back control of Tigray’s government . It restored the regional legislature that existed before the war and installed Gebremichael as regional president.
On Sunday, the TPLF joined six other armed groups in a new alliance seeking to remove Abiy’s government and establish a transitional administration. The alliance includes former enemies who fought on opposite sides of the last war.
TPLF spokesman Michael Asgedom told the Associated Press the groups would cooperate politically and militarily. Asked whether joining the alliance violated the Pretoria agreement, Asgedom said the accord was “no longer valid.”
The Amhara Fano National Movement fought alongside the federal government against the TPLF during the last war, then turned against it in 2023. The Oromo Liberation Army, which has long fought Abiy’s government in Oromia, is also a member.
Reuters reported Wednesday that Tigrayan forces were fighting alongside the Fano group in Amhara and a local armed group in Afar.
But Getahun questioned how long the alliance would hold.
The TPLF and Fano remain divided over contested territory, particularly Western Tigray, and its members have different political and military goals.
“This is a temporary marriage of convenience against a mutual enemy rather than a lasting political agreement,” he said.
Abiy’s spokesperson, Billene Seyoum, told Reuters on Monday that the groups had already been working together with financial backing from Eritrea. Relations between Ethiopia and Eritrea have deteriorated since their forces fought together in the last war, though the Eritrean government has repeatedly denied supporting Ethiopian armed groups.
The African Union (AU) said Wednesday that the airport seizures were inconsistent with the Pretoria deal and urged both parties to de-escalate. It also asked for help from former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, who helped mediate the 2022 agreement.
Tigray has yet to recover from the last war, with communities still rebuilding and many displaced people still unable to return home.
Ethiopia is already dealing with armed conflicts in Amhara and Oromia, and ACLED says the federal military was “stretched” before the renewed fighting with the TPLF. But the armed groups in the new alliance vary in their fighting capacity, with several lacking the organization or recruits for wider operations and others largely confined to local areas, according to the conflict monitor.
There is also the risk of Eritrea’s military becoming involved. Tensions have grown between the two countries over Ethiopia’s push for access to the Red Sea , including through Eritrea’s port of Assab. The AU urged Ethiopia’s neighbors to avoid actions that could fuel the conflict.
The region is already grappling with the war in Sudan and longstanding tensions between Ethiopia, Egypt and Sudan over the Nile.
Getahun warned that the current fighting could become even more devastating than the previous conflict.
“A renewed war would likely end up far bloodier and more widespread than the 2020–2022 fighting,” he said.
“Immediate de-escalation and dialogue” are now essential, he added, arguing that negotiations remain “the only viable path forward.”

articles.title_orig: New Jersey Gov. Sherrill calls on her lieutenant governor to resign
articles.title_zh: New Jersey Gov. Sherrill calls on her lieutenant governor to resign
articles.content_orig:
New Jersey’s governor called on her hand-picked lieutenant governor to resign by Friday after a law firm hired by her office concluded he behaved inappropriately around women.
The firm’s report published Wednesday found that Dale Caldwell violated the state’s policy prohibiting discrimination in the workplace. It said he made an advance toward a staffer’s friend and when he was rebuffed, he told the staffer, “you young women are looking for young sperm.”
“The investigation found that the Lieutenant Governor engaged in serious, repeated violations of state policy and failed to uphold the responsibilities of his office,” Gov. Mikie Sherrill said in a statement Thursday.
Caldwell’s lawyer, Thomas Calcagni, disputed the allegations, calling the investigation a one-sided operation that did not include necessary due process.
“The Lieutenant Governor was not provided a meaningful opportunity to address each of these anonymous allegations,” he said in a statement.
Caldwell “categorically denies” making the alleged statement about women wanting sperm, the lawyer said, adding that a state police trooper who was present at the time didn’t hear it said.
The report also accused Caldwell of breaking the state’s ethics rules by trying to get a promotion for a state employee he was dating.
In May, Caldwell emailed an unnamed official recommending his romantic partner, who he called a friend, for a promotion to a leadership position, the report said. He included her resume and a letter she sent expressing interest in a senior leadership position, according to the report.
Calcagni acknowledged that Caldwell had recommended a promotion for a woman with whom he had a personal relationship, but said he believed she was qualified for the job and hadn’t ordered anyone to promote her.
“There is a difference between failing to disclose a personal relationship when forwarding the resume of a qualified job applicant and actually using the power of public office to secure a job or financial benefit for someone,” Calcagni said.
The report also found seven ticketed events between Feb. 19 and May 23 where Caldwell reportedly brought one or more guests without paying for them. The events included one at the State Opera of New Jersey and a Rowan University Rosa Parks Scholarship Luncheon, with tickets ranging from $65 to $300, according to the report.
“Where a sponsor waives admission to an event for an official’s family member, friend, or date, the value of that admission is an impermissible benefit to the official,” the report said.
In May, Caldwell sent a message responding to accusations of ethical violations against him. He denied several claims, including that he gives out his businesses cards to women for inappropriate reasons, calling that “categorically untrue.”
“Unfortunately, in this current political environment, false accusations, especially against people of color, seem to be commonplace,” Caldwell, who is Black, wrote.
Sherrill, a Democrat, said Caldwell’s “ethical lapses” continued even with multiple warnings and trainings. She called his resignation “in the best interest of New Jersey residents.”
“These violations substantiated in the investigation reflect a pattern of behavior that does not meet the standards of this Administration,” she said.
A Methodist pastor, Caldwell was president of Centenary University for two years before being elected lieutenant governor, a post that has existed in New Jersey for around 20 years.
While candidates for governor get to pick the people who will appear on the ticket as their running mate, and serve as lieutenant governor, it is an independently elected position.
New Jersey’s governor cannot fire Caldwell. She has the power to assign, or remove, him from certain responsibilities, and could effectively sideline him from playing an active role in state government. But lieutenant governors can be impeached and removed from office by the Legislature.
As lieutenant governor, Caldwell is first in line to become the governor if Sherrill were to die, be removed from office or become incapacitated. The lieutenant governor’s office, while more than ceremonial, is largely subservient to the governor.

articles.title_orig: WNBA playoffs 2026: How all eight teams could win the title
articles.title_zh: WNBA playoffs 2026: How all eight teams could win the title
articles.content_orig:
The chaos of the final day of the WNBA regular season, which decided three of the four first-round playoff matchups, feels like a scaled-down harbinger of what’s next. We’re about to see an unusually wide-open first round; the gap between the no. 1 and no. 8 seeds is a historically tight seven games. For reference, that gap was 11 games last season and 17 the season before. Every lower seed boasts a little bit of a “nobody wants to see them in the first round” factor, besides the injury-plagued Dallas Wings, who carry the inferior but still scary “nothing to lose” label.
The WNBA’s 30th regular season has also been its longest, and the home-away-home format of the first round (which isn't organized by conference) will guarantee arduous travel for six of eight playoff teams. To boot, half the league is still getting over the jet lag and interruption caused by the FIBA tournament earlier this month in Berlin, held smack-dab in the final third of the WNBA season. There has never been a better time for an underdog to steal a game—or even a series.
I hesitate to romanticize the WNBA’s shoestring-budget past, but there’s something quaint about a season marked by exponential increases in player salaries hearkening back to the league’s adaptive, provisional roots. In time, the first round will be longer, and once expansion is complete, conferences will likely be reinstated as a structuring part of postseason play. But for now, in the messy middle of the WNBA’s ascendance , we are being given the gift of a rare first round where just about anything could happen—which has both its charms and frustrations.
With that in mind, let’s rank the first-round series based on the likelihood of an upset, starting with the longest shot, and examine the postseason race as a whole.
Paige Bueckers controls the ball against Gabby Williams
Dallas is the great afterthought of the postseason, and rightfully so. It has been absolutely decimated by injuries. Azzi Fudd, the 2026 no. 1 pick and the Wings’ best point-of-attack defender, is out for the rest of the season. The status of Alanna Smith, whose rim protection has carried a team to the WNBA Finals before, remains up in the air.
But they do have two wild cards:
I don’t see Dallas winning this series, but I wouldn’t be surprised if it kept up against the Valkyries’ style longer than expected.
One more stat: Dallas’s new starting lineup has the best offensive rating in the WNBA.
Breanna Stewart, Olivia Miles, and Han Xu go up for a rebound
When Sabrina Ionescu told reporters recently that New York isn’t your traditional eighth seed, she wasn’t just offering feigned optimism. The Liberty defeated the Lynx in five (controversial) games in the 2024 WNBA Finals, and the 26-18 record they clawed their way to this season—despite injuries to Ionescu, Satou Sabally (who is out for the year), Leonie Fiebich, and more—would have been good enough for the no. 5 seed last year.
The Lynx would have been a shoo-in to beat nearly any of the other lower seeds, but they've historically (and recently) struggled against New York's size.

As we found out in their last matchup, Fiebich and Breanna Stewart are one of the only duos with the size, speed, and versatility to switch an Olivia Miles–Napheesa Collier pick-and-roll.
With Collier back in the starting lineup, the Lynx are better as a whole than they were before her return—averaging a plus-18.5 net rating—but Collier adds some subtle wrinkles that could prove advantageous for New York. With Natasha Howard setting the bulk of Miles’s screens, the pick-and-roll had turned into a perpetual layup line for Minnesota. With Collier back, the Lynx have become more jumper-happy, partially because the two-time MVP runner-up gets double-teamed constantly. On its own, adding a little bit of variance to fuel a scintillating offense isn’t a bad thing. But the Lynx are also giving up five more points in the paint than they were before Collier’s return from her ankle surgeries. The five-time All-Star simply isn’t at 100 percent yet—by her own admission—and her gradual return to form has naturally taken a toll on Minnesota’s physicality in the paint, an area where it has to put forth a full-throttle effort to make up for its lack of defensive size.
One more stat: The Lynx are in the bottom three in the WNBA in points in the paint since Collier’s return .
Kiki Iriafen drives to the basket against Angel Reese
Hey, Washington: Get Angel Reese in foul trouble. She is frankly Atlanta’s only line of defense against the Mystics’ three-headed frontcourt monster of Kiki Iriafen, Shakira Austin, and Lauren Betts. The Dream are 7.9 points per 100 possessions worse defensively when Reese sits, and there’s a steep drop-off when her backups, even DeWanna Bonner, enter the game.
The Mystics and the Dream have similar styles. At a time when the rest of the WNBA is trending toward guard play and offense, both are in the top three in defensive rating, points in the paint, second-chance points, and free throw attempts. But in a war of attrition, the team with the most bodies—and, therefore, the most contingency plans—wins, and that’s the Mystics. For the Mystics, the youngest team in the WNBA, this is an opportunity to call shots, take names, form an identity, and prove that they are formidable as well as fun.
One more stat: The Mystics may be ranked 12th on offense, but they have the no. 1 free throw rate in the WNBA.
Caitlin Clark is guarded by A’ja Wilson and Jewell Loyd
The Aces and the Fever have similar makeups: a Big Three, questionable depth made worse by crushing injuries, and maddening defensive inconsistency. The Aces have lost NaLyssa Smith, A’ja Wilson’s frontcourt mate and a legit Most Improved Player candidate, for the season due to a knee injury. The Fever, meanwhile, await potentially devastating news on the status of Ty Harris, who had to be carried off the court in the final game of the regular season because of an ankle injury. Aliyah Boston also left that game early with a leg injury that has hampered her nearly all season long.
With Caitlin Clark and Kelsey Mitchell, Indiana has the best-scoring backcourt of all time. The Aces, on the other hand, have such putrid perimeter defense that Becky Hammon is starting essentially a one-way player in Stephanie Talbot, who has logged eight zero-point games this season. With Smith out, Hammon will likely have to go small around Wilson, exacerbating the Aces’ defensive issues. Per Synergy, nobody has given up more points as a primary defender this season than the Aces’ Jackie Young. Jewell Loyd, at 11th worst, is not far behind. The Fever have their own perimeter deficiencies on the defensive end, and I wouldn’t blame you for picking the team featuring the GOAT and the title pedigree to win here. But if the series turns into a defense-optional, offense-optimal free-for-all, I’m siding with Indiana, which has broken the 100-point mark this season more than any other team in WNBA history.
One more stat: The Aces’ Big Three of Wilson, Young, and Chelsea Gray have logged 243 games together (postseason included).

Anyone who’s not keen on a congressional investigation into the WNBA. The prospect of a Fever-Dream matchup in the first round, with its on- and off-court combustibility, had me feeling pre-exhausted. On paper, a Fever-Dream rematch featuring Clark versus Reese—with the added juice of Bonner returning to Indiana after leaving the team just five games into last season—should be the stuff of a sportswriter’s dreams. In reality, the first inkling of conflict (inevitable, by the way) would have hung a discourse anchor around the first round. Anyway, now that we have avoided that crisis

articles.title_orig: ‘America’s Bishop’ Was Beatified. 50,000 Catholics Showed Up.
articles.title_zh: ‘America’s Bishop’ Was Beatified. 50,000 Catholics Showed Up.
articles.content_orig:
Send your thoughts to Letters to the Editor . Learn more
In the former home of the NFL’s St. Louis Rams on Thursday Sept. 24, there was an unusual option beside the popcorn and soft drinks: T-shirts bearing the face of a Catholic archbishop.
Tens of thousands of attendees filled The Dome at America’s Center and many more joined online to view the formal, lengthy ceremony celebrating the beatification of Archbishop Fulton Sheen — who now holds the title "blessed" and is one step closer to sainthood. Sometimes called the first televangelist in the United States, Sheen’s beatification was presided over by Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, a media star in the Philippines and a Vatican evangelization official.
It came after the Vatican determined Sheen had lived a life of "heroic virtue" and that a mother’s 2010 prayer for Sheen’s intercession was responsible for the miraculous recovery of her baby, James Fulton Engstrom, who spent 61 minutes without a heartbeat after birth.
Sheen, who died in 1979, beat out Lucille Ball for the Emmy Award for Most Outstanding Personality in 1953. His radio show, "The Catholic Hour," and television shows, including "Life Is Worth Living" reached millions. Pope Leo XIV has said that he grew up listening to Sheen.
On Thursday, before the Mass, thousands of priests, nuns and faithful milled around a crowded and sweaty expo hall examining Sheen car magnets and buying rosaries. Some ventured to the next hall to attend confession. Some listened to a pre-show with worship music by Christian musician Matt Maher and reflections by prominent Catholic figures, including Peoria, Illinois, Bishop Louis Tylka and retired New York Cardinal Timothy Dolan, with both bishops representing locations key to Sheen’s life.
As the procession began, orchestral music spilled out and incense wafted through the air, and hundreds of priests and bishops passed. They all were wearing white chasubles, liturgical vestments, embroidered with a golden "JMJ" on their back, a nod to Sheen’s habit of scrawling the initials for Jesus, Mary and Joseph at the top of a blackboard during his popular TV show.
The multilingual Mass included Spanish, Portuguese, English, French, Chinese, Tagalog and Vietnamese.
In his homily, Tagle preached against priests " proclaiming destructive words and doing violent acts" and evangelizers who are "self-affirming." As he spoke to a largely U.S. crowd, Tagle quoted extensively from Sheen’s address to the Second Vatican Council, where the Sheen raised concerns about poverty in Africa, Asia and Latin America.
" To preach the gospel from a posture of self-righteousness that prevents you from empathizing with other people’s brokenness is not mission," said Tagle. " Blessed is the missionary who digs deep into the heart of the poor to meet Jesus there."
After the Mass concluded, attendees lined up to venerate Sheen’s mandible, or jaw bone.
" It’s quite stunning to think that the jaw that moved up and down in front of millions to bring the gospel, we now get to stand in front of and say, ‘Pray for us,’" said Katie Prejean McGrady, the Catholic author and radio host, from the stage before the Mass.
Many Catholics said they traveled hours to witness the festivities. The Rev. Marek Piedziewicz from the Diocese of Elbląg, Poland, said it took him 30 hours to reach St. Louis. He learned about Sheen over a decade ago when he saw Polish young people wearing Sheen T-shirts — Sheen’s work became popular there after being translated into Polish. " He is very popular in Poland," he told RNS, adding he has gone on to write three books about Sheen.
" This is the consequence of this contact with the T-shirt," he said.
Several said they hoped Sheen’s beatification would inspire greater devotion to Jesus Christ.
The Rev. Ray Buehler from St. Louis’ Assumption-Mattese parish said, "Fulton Sheen really, in a beautiful way, exemplifies what engaging in the media rightly can do to advance our Lord’s kingdom — that there is this sort of humility and love and courage that he embraced it with."
Buehler also called Winona-Rochester, Minnesota, Bishop Robert Barron, who preached at a vespers service the evening before, a "modern-day Fulton Sheen." He said he appreciated Barron’s reminder that Sheen is already in heaven. "He doesn’t really need our admiration. But if anything, it’s just a reminder to all of us that all of us are called to holiness," said Buehler of Barron’s homily.
At the vespers service, Barron said , "Anyone who seeks fresh language to bring the gospel to our culture, anyone who preaches the ancient word with a heart on fire, anyone who dares to use the media of communication available to us today, is indebted to Fulton Sheen and finds in him a powerful heavenly friend and intercessor."
With the beatification Mass complete, the Vatican can now begin to investigate potential miracles that qualify for sainthood; Sheen just needs one more for canonization.
"The good news is that Pope Francis originally signed off for the beatification to happen in 2019, and anything reported from the time Pope Francis signed off on a miracle can be considered now for the second miracle for canonization," said Tylka. He said he believes there are already six reported miracles the Vatican can begin to investigate.
Dayspring Brock, a teacher from Dallas, said she anticipated that the day would continue to impact her. "I’m just really open to seeing what graces might come of being here and witnessing this amazing person just being recognized as a wonderful witness for us all."
Several Catholics said they hoped the bishop and theology professor would be remembered most for his deep devotion to prayer. Sheen’s example of praying for an hour a day before the Eucharist — a practice called the Holy Hour — helped popularize the devotion.
"Spoiler alert, this is all about the glory of God," Sister Josephine Garrett, one of the Sisters of the Holy Family of Nazareth, told attendees at a pre-show. "The stadium, the pop-ups, the screens, the chairs, the decorations is about giving glory to God for what he did in one man because he always makes good on his promises."

articles.title_orig: I Tested the Apple Watch's New Heart Rate Sensor to See If It's Really Better Than Garmin's
articles.title_zh: I Tested the Apple Watch's New Heart Rate Sensor to See If It's Really Better Than Garmin's
articles.content_orig:
Apple caught my attention with their claim that the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 have the “most accurate heart rate in a wearable.” It’s hard to make a really accurate heart rate sensor, and in my experience, Apple hasn’t had a great track record in that area. So I tested the Series 12 pretty intensively over the past week or so, and now I have results.
I’m picky about accuracy; longtime readers have seen me test watch after watch against my trusty chest strap to find out how good each one really is. That sometimes brings surprises: The Powerbeats Pro 2 are surprisingly bad at heart rate tracking if you have small ears, for example. I also discovered that the Garmin Forerunner 570 is shockingly good at heart rate accuracy, far better than any other device I had tested up to that point. (Garmin’s Forerunner 970 and the newest Fenix and Venu watches have the same sensor.)
Is the new Apple Watch really good enough to beat Garmin’s best sensor? Apple believes it is, but I doubted that claim, for a few reasons. The first is simply Apple’s track record. Early models of the Apple watch had better sensors than most wearables at the time, so Apple developed a reputation for good accuracy. For example, back in 2019 or so, the Series 4 watch performed far better for me than the Whoop 3.0. But time marches on, and devices have gotten better. Garmin has an excellent sensor, as I already explained; the Pixel watch is also impressively good. But Apple just didn’t keep up.
You can see it in my comparisons over the years: here’s the Series 11 glitching where a Garmin did just fine, and here’s the Series 10 struggling alongside a Fitbit Charge 6. If I were to rank all the heart rate sensors I’ve tested for their accuracy, the Garmin 570 would be A-tier, the Pixel Watch and most good sports watches would get a B, and the Apple Watch (Series 10 and 11) would be a C. (S-tier would be reserved for chest straps.) Not long ago, I got downvoted to negative infinity for commenting on Reddit that Apple’s heart rate accuracy (up to the Series 11) is “mid at best.” Sorry, but it’s true.
But, OK, perhaps it’s a new era. Apple redesigned its optical heart rate sensor to include larger LEDs and arrange them more closely in a circle. To support its claim that the new sensor is the most accurate on the market, it published a study that was extensive in its breadth (seven recent, competing devices were tested in a variety of activities) but limited in usefulness. Each pairing of a device and workout type was given, essentially, one number. We don’t get to see how each device behaves in use. The data feels cherry-picked, and in any case, it doesn’t give us enough information to say whether one sensor is truly better than another, or specifically what it does better. So I’m going to add my own data points.
I am just one person, so my experiments amount to a very small, informal study. That’s the case for any tech reviewer, no matter their qualifications—so feel free to compare my data to what others have found, but keep these limitations in mind for each of us.
I took the Apple Watch Series 12 and the Garmin Forerunner 570 out for several tests during workouts. (I did not have a feasible way of testing background measurements outside of workouts.) I wore one device on each wrist, positioned according to manufacturer recommendations, and, at the same time, used an electrical chest strap to provide the reference values.
I have relatively light skin, which may improve accuracy, and no wrist tattoos, so both sensors should get a clear signal on either wrist. I have six-inch wrists, on the small side of average, so I wore the 42-millimeter size of each watch (both are available in larger sizes for those who prefer it). A good fit is critical to getting good accuracy, and I feel I achieved that for both devices. I did my best to have both devices equally snug (but not uncomfortably tight) against my wrist.
I tested both devices, together, on treadmill runs, outdoor trail runs, a rowing session, and a few strength sessions. Some of these workouts involved quick changes in intensity, leading to peaks and troughs in the graph. Others were more steady. Gripping objects such as dumbbells or rower handles can interfere with accuracy for some devices, which is why I included those workouts. Ambient light and temperature can affect accuracy as well, so I tested in a variety of weather conditions.
In my first set of tests, which I also shared here , the Apple Watch and the Garmin both performed well, but each had their flaws. The Garmin sometimes lagged a bit at the start of the interval, but quickly caught up. The Apple Watch didn’t have that problem, but sometimes missed the highest values on small spikes in heart rate. I’d call this one a tie.
In my other trail runs and treadmill runs, I saw a similar pattern: Both watches would be on track most of the time, but each had their quirks. Garmin was more likely to miss out on the beginning of spikes, but the Apple Watch was more likely to drop data points entirely, especially toward the beginning of a workout.
One day, I did three mini workouts at the gym: a treadmill run, a rowing session, and a strength session. The strength work included a few sets each of overhead barbell press, front squats (with my arms in a clean grip), and dumbbell curls. On the rower, the Garmin struggled more, missing almost half of the second interval. The Apple Watch wasn’t perfect, though, overestimating in a few places and not always picking up the lowest value between intervals.
The strength workout was a mess for both devices. The Garmin often read low, but the Apple Watch sometimes read high and reported fewer values in total. This view shows it a bit better (each data point is a dot):
Looking at my data, I think the biggest news is that Apple is no longer lagging when it comes to heart rate accuracy. The Series 12 is a lot more accurate in my tests than the Series 10 or 11 ever were. Apple has built a very good heart rate sensor, and they deserve huge credit for that. I will no longer have to tell people Apple's sensor is mid.
But does it have the best heart rate sensor? I’m not so sure I’m convinced. It is holding its own against Garmin’s best sensor, for sure, and that’s impressive. In the rare cases the Garmin struggles, the Apple is usually there with a more-or-less correct value. But I have seen near-perfect graphs from the Garmin on its best days (admittedly, outside of this testing week); I've never seen one quite like that from Apple. The Apple Watch's sensor sometimes has trouble ramping up to correct values at the beginning of a workout; it overestimates on occasion; it doesn’t get all the way down to low values when intervals change quickly; and I’m concerned about the sparseness of the data points. And if we truly want to compare the Apple Watch to all wearables, shouldn’t we consider chest straps, which are also worn, and which are objectively more accurate than any optical sensor in a watch?

articles.title_zh: Macron denies CIA warned France of Russian drone attack
articles.content_orig:
French President Emmanuel Macron denied CIA warnings of a possible Russian drone operation targeting southern Europe and pledged Thursday to send "military assets" to "protect" the Yanbu site, a key component of Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure network on Thursday.
In a joint interview aired on broadcasters France 2 and TF1 he said "We can deny this piece of information, the CIA did not inform France of this information and the Italian defence minister said the same thing".
On Thursday, Spanish daily newspaper El Mundo published an article which declared that the CIA had alerted several southern European governments to a possible Russian drone operation targeting Spain, France and Italy.
Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto subsequently denied these allegations on Thursday, declaring on X that "the alarm raised this morning by a Spanish newspaper that hypothesises possible attacks on Italy, Spain, and France by Russian ships and drones serves no one and is not confirmed."
"We already live in difficult, 'nervous' times, and no one needs more fuel on the fire", he added.
Macron also affirmed that France would send "military assets" to "protect" the Yanbu site of the East-West pipeline on the Red Sea, which provides Saudi Arabia with an alternative route for transporting crude and refined oil to European markets.
He detailed that this would amount to "military assets, meaning troops, radar systems, and defensive systems to protect this site, but we will not be engaging in any conflict. Our aim is to help stabilise the oil market."
The pipeline has played a crucial role during the war in the Middle East, allowing Saudi Arabia to bypass the Strait of Hormuz to export its oil. It can transport 5 million barrels of crude oil per day, with the capacity to temporarily increase to 7 million barrels.
The port, which also houses significant oil storage and refining facilities, has become a target for Houthi forces in Yemen, backed by Iran, during the current conflict in the Middle East.
"As soon as one of these locations is relaxed, the immediate impact is seen at the gas pump," the head of state added. "You'll see it in two days."
Hard-left France Unbowed leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon reacted to plans to mobilise military assets by calling for a parliamentary vote on the issue.
“Sending troops to Saudi Arabia means entering a theatre of war. If the base is attacked, what will we do? There’s no question of becoming a belligerent party," Mélenchon said.
Addressing Russia's ongoing and intensifying hybrid campaign against Europe, Macron referred to the drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport on the night of 4-5 August 2026, which German authorities have attributed to Russia.
Macron said France had not experienced a comparable attack so far but warned that one remained possible. "When you ask me, 'Could this happen?' my answer is yes," he said.
The French President stressed that Russia considers “Europe to be the strategic heart of Ukraine," while also saying that the possibility of Russia seeking to launch an attack against Europe was "plausible."
"It is clear that there have been several signs indicating that Russia is preparing to do this," he stated.
As speculation mounts over Russia’s possible mobilisation plans, Macron said that a new mobilisation of around 300,000 personnel was a “credible scenario” that was “often shared”.
The French leader said he viewed this as a sign that Moscow was prepared to "make even greater sacrifices to take over the entire Donbas", estimating that Russia would need to advance for “a year and a half, two years” at the current pace to conquer the territories it does not yet control in that region, “with terrible losses and suffering for Ukraine.”

articles.title_orig: China swimmer makes Asian Games history as Thai sprinter wins track 100m
articles.title_zh: China swimmer makes Asian Games history as Thai sprinter wins track 100m
articles.content_orig:
Towering teenager Zhang Zhanshuo became the first swimmer in history to win seven golds at a single Asian Games, while on the track, Thai sprinter Puripol Boonson powered to victory in the 100m.
China’s Zhang, 19, scorched to the men’s 400m freestyle title in the pool in Tokyo on Friday in a Games-record three minutes and 41.28 seconds.
He sat on the lane divider after the race and slowly counted off on his fingers all seven medals he had won.
Zhang also won individual golds in the 200m, 800m and 1,500m freestyle events, as well as three relays.
He said, after wrapping up a scintillating campaign, that it had been the “perfect week”.
“I think the most important thing is to stay grounded and focused, because the Asian Games are not my ultimate goal,” said Zhang, who stands 198cm (six feet, six inches).
With the Los Angeles Olympics less than two years away, China won 30 of the 42 golds in the pool this week.
Their 13-year-old phenomenon Yu Zidi was the undoubted superstar, taking home three individual golds and all in Games-record times.
Not to be outdone, Japan’s 17-year-old Shin Ohashi shattered the men’s 200m breaststroke world record on Thursday.
Swimming, equestrian and diving are taking place in Tokyo, but the city of Nagoya and the wider Aichi prefecture are the main Games host.
The men’s and women’s 100m sprints, the blue riband events in track and field, took place in front of rows of empty seats in Nagoya.
China’s Chen Yujie streaked to a comfortable victory in the women’s final in a Games-record 11.06 seconds.
The men’s was won by 20-year-old Puripol, who burst out of the pack in the final quarter of the race to win in 9.90 seconds, breaking his Games record from earlier in the evening.
It was Thailand’s first men’s 100m gold medal since Suchart Jairsuraparp on home soil at the 1978 Bangkok Games.
On the last evening of gymnastics, Carlos Yulo won the men’s vault for his second gold of the Games.
The double Olympic champion won floor gold on Thursday to complete his collection of major titles.
“I can’t believe it,” the Filipino said.
“In this whole Asian Games, I felt really stressed, but at the same time, I enjoyed what I did today. I really did my part.
“Today was really a miracle for me.”
There’s little time to celebrate, however, with the world championships next month.
South Korea edged China 85-80 in the semifinals of the women’s basketball, and will face hosts Japan for gold.
China had their giant centre Zhang Ziyu, 19, but it was not enough.
Zhang Ziyu stands 223cm (seven feet, four inches) and scored 22 points.
“She was tough to guard,” said South Korea’s Kang Lee-seul.
“We couldn’t defend her, but we focused on fast breaks and shooting more three-pointers.”
North Korea’s women were again in record-setting form on the weightlifting dais.
Oh Kwang Ok set three world records on her way to women’s 57kg bodyweight class gold.
Oh lifted 104kg in the snatch and 134kg in the clean and jerk for a 238kg total – all world records to add to the two golds North Korea’s women won in the 49kg and 53kg classes this week.
North Korea has won four gold medals and two silvers in the six weightlifting events contested so far.

“This move is a diplomatic all-timer,” Santi Ruiz, a policy-focused writer for the Institute for Progress and editorial team member at AI company Anthropic, posted on X. “It's like Messi cutting inside. You know it’s coming. It doesn’t matter how many times they run it. You’re getting those pandas, and you’ll like it.”
The tried-and-tested offering came once again on Thursday as Chinese President Xi Jinping announced during his state visit to the U.S. that Ping Ping and Fu Shuang , two giant pandas from a research base in Chengdu, would be lent to Zoo Atlanta in the state of Georgia—but whether this so-called panda diplomacy remains as welcome as it has over the decades is less clear, eliciting mixed reactions in 2026.
The practice gained traction after the National Zoo received giant pandas from Beijing in the wake of President Richard Nixon and First Lady Pat Nixon’s historic trip to China in 1972, which marked a new, positive chapter in U.S.-China relations.
China claims ownership of nearly all the giant pandas in the world, even their offspring, and controls who receives them. Beijing eventually shifted from gifting giant pandas to leasing them to other countries in 1984 as the animal’s population dwindled, but the practice continued and spread to other nations like Austria, Canada, and Malaysia. China regularly considers loaning pandas an act of goodwill—even when the host nation typically foots the bill of about $1 million annually for a pair.
A giant panda’s presence or absence in a country tends to represent ebbs and flows of its relationship with China. For instance, amid tensions with Japan over Taiwan , Tokyo returned two giant pandas to Sichuan on loan in January, marking the first time Japan does not have a giant panda since 1972, when China-Japan ties first normalized. In 2010, two U.S.-born panda cubs returned to China , days after Chinese officials warned then-President Barack Obama against meeting the Dalai Lama, whom Beijing considers a separatist.
“No other animal has been turned into a symbol to the extent that pandas have been,” says Czeslaw Tubilewicz, a senior lecturer at Adelaide University.
It’s also no coincidence that Zoo Atlanta received the giant pandas, Tubilewicz says, as the gift represented Beijing’s appreciation of Georgia’s historical economic partnership with China on several aspects: “When most southern states, especially Republican states, turned very negative on China, Georgia continued its pro-China policy consistently. So when it comes to those pandas, and in [Zoo Atlanta], in a way, Xi Jinping is trying to kill two birds with two pandas.”
But China’s transformation from a developing economy to one of the world’s superpowers has also raised questions about whether the gesture of sending giant pandas still works. China is massively different from how it used to be in the 1970s, and is currently embroiled in a wide range of issues, not only with the U.S., but also with other countries, which makes categorizing it neatly as a friend or foe less easy.
Ja Ian Chong, associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore, tells TIME that “the image of the pandas as soft, friendly, and cuddly—they don’t work today because a lot of [China’s aggressive] actions now are a lot more visible and fresh in people’s minds.”
“No one cares about pandas when national security or geostrategic interests come into play,” Tubilewicz added.
A 2022 peer-reviewed study at the University of Connecticut found that U.S. students who viewed panda videos that were not sourced from the government were likely to have a positive attitude toward Chinese culture and, in turn, Chinese people.
But while China’s practice of leasing pandas gives some people warm feelings, it makes others hot with anger. Conservationists and animal advocates have argued against using pandas as geopolitical pawns. Following the South Korea-China Summit earlier this year, the countries’ respective environmental officials discussed additional giant panda loans. But a Korean animal rights group slammed the move , saying that the creatures “are not beings born for human entertainment or interstate friendship.”
And many others are also starting to look past the panda diplomacy and demand other measures. A 2026 survey of U.S. adults conducted by NORC at the University of Chicago found that 28% of respondents said sending pandas to American zoos would improve their view of China, but much higher percentages said that more concrete actions like Chinese cooperation on curbing fentanyl precursors or easing trade restrictions would improve their view of China.
“The symbolism was still dominant in the 1970s,” Chong said. “It’s just that, given the lack of information, given the environment of that time, the symbolism probably got a lot more traction before than today.”
While surveys show many Americans are warming to China , Chong says “deep reservoirs of reservations remain,” particularly among Trump’s MAGA base: a July survey from the Chicago Council on Global Affairs says that 63% of MAGA Republicans favor limiting the growth of Chinese power.
“Affection for pandas does not automatically translate into support for Chinese government policies,” Yu Tao, associate professor in Chinese Studies at the University of Western Australia, tells TIME. “Its more realistic contribution is to sustain public goodwill and opportunities for cooperation. The strongest case for panda diplomacy is that it gives people something they want to preserve in a relationship otherwise defined pretty much by disputes.”

“We had a great meeting,” Trump said later that afternoon at the Southern Portico, where he gave Xi a tour of the South Lawn Helipad .
“He’s an expert on stones, and he loves good granite,” Trump said of Xi.
The day began with remarks from both Trump and Xi at the grand foyer of the White House. Afterward, Trump and Xi participated in a military review at the Rose Garden and took part in hours of meetings before Trump led a tour of parts of the White House.
While both leaders mentioned AI in their opening remarks, Xi stressed that the development of AI always needs to be “under human control.”
Trump was set to host a state dinner for Xi Thursday evening, joined by a slate of tech leaders. Amazon Executive Chairman Jeff Bezos, Google CEO Sundar Pichai, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla CEO Elon Musk were set to attend the dinner, a White House official confirmed.
According to Chinese state media, President Xi raised the issue of Iran during the bilateral meeting, saying that he hoped the US and Iran would resume negotiations and that China would support the two countries recommitting to the 14-point memorandum of understanding reached months ago.
On Taiwan, Xi said he hopes the U.S. would maintain its position of opposing Taiwan independence. The U.S. has not officially endorsed Taiwan's independence, but has previously sold weaponry to the island and is widely viewed as a key player if China were to ever invade the self-ruling island.
Earlier on Thursday, Xi urged more cooperation between the two countries. During his remarks, he called for more direct flights between the U.S. and China and invited 100,000 American students for cultural exchange in the next five years. And continuing a longtime diplomatic tradition stretching back to the Nixon era, he announced two pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be delivered to Zoo Atlanta in the coming days.
“China and the United States must hold the line of no conflict and no confrontation between us, and we can certainly find the right path for two great countries to get along on this planet we both call home,” Xi said.
This is the first time a Chinese leader has made a second formal state visit to America. The last time Xi conducted a formal state visit in Washington, D.C. was at the invitation of President Obama in September 2015, three years after he succeeded as the General Secretary of the Chinese Communist Party.
Trump and Xi first met in 2017, during Trump’s first term, at the President’s home base of Mar-a-Lago, Florida. The pair last met in May during a two-day state visit by Trump to Beijing, where the U.S. and China delegations discussed a range of topics including tariffs, rare mineral trade, as well as the Strait of Hormuz. The two leaders used the visit to announce the launch of a so-called Board of Trade intended to lower tariffs on products that aren’t considered a national security risk. In June, the Office of the United States Trade Representative asked the public to weigh in on which types of products would benefit from this new mechanism. articles.title_orig: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China
articles.title_zh: Pomp over progress in Xi’s US summit with Trump is a win for China
articles.content_orig:
While US president hailed visit as ‘great’, almost nothing of substance was achieved on resolving thorny issues
Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in Washington
If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “ stalemate summit ”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs.
Instead, it was described as a celebration of “ diplotainment ” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo.
Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”.
“The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration.
But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.
One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China.
To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year.
With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year.
That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029.
On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society.
William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”.
China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.
Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.”
Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights.
On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”.
For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely.
On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want ​to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.”
For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

articles.title_zh: Details on US, China Trade Talks to Come on Monday, Says Greer
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Friday that the U.S. and China have reached agreements covering a subset of goods the two countries can trade on more favorable terms, marking fresh progress in negotiations between the world's two largest economies.
"We've actually reached agreement with the Chinese on a number of these things," Greer said on CNBC's "Squawk Box," referring to goods including U.S. agricultural products and medical devices and Chinese consumer goods considered non-sensitive.
Greer said the Trump administration plans to release "a lot more details" Monday about what the two sides have accomplished in negotiations over the past several weeks. He said the goal is to carve out areas of trade that could remain insulated from future tariff measures or broader trade disputes.
The two countries want some goods to be traded on a "more preferential basis" and potentially left aside if either country imposes new tariffs.
Greer did not specify Friday which products are covered by the agreements, how tariffs on those goods could change or when the new terms would take effect. articles.title_orig: Details on U.S.-China trade negotiations coming Monday, USTR Greer says
articles.title_zh: Details on U.S.-China trade negotiations coming Monday, USTR Greer says
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC on Friday that the U.S. and China have reached agreements covering a subset of goods the two countries can trade on more favorable terms, marking fresh progress in negotiations between the world's two largest economies.
"We've actually reached agreement with the Chinese on a number of these things," Greer said on CNBC's "Squawk Box," referring to goods including U.S. agricultural products and medical devices and Chinese consumer goods considered non-sensitive.
Greer said the Trump administration plans to release "a lot more details" Monday about what the two sides have accomplished in negotiations over the past several weeks. He said the goal is to carve out areas of trade that could remain insulated from future tariff measures or broader trade disputes.
The two countries want some goods to be traded on a "more preferential basis" and potentially left aside if either country imposes new tariffs.
Greer did not specify Friday which products are covered by the agreements, how tariffs on those goods could change or when the new terms would take effect. Negotiations under the new U.S.-China "Board of Trade" mechanism are focused on "pure trade issues," Greer said, rather than U.S. national security restrictions on advanced technology.
"All those export controls that are national security issues, we take those off the table," Greer said.
Trump and Xi, after they met in Beijing in May, announced the establishment of the "Board of Trade" to manage trade between the two rivals in non-sensitive products. Businesses have been waiting for more details on what categories of trade would be set aside, under the new framework, for lower tariffs.
The news come as Washington and Beijing have also agreed to extend their broader trade truce by two months, giving the two sides more time to negotiate over longstanding economic disputes.
Greer said Friday that the U.S. views those two months as "compliance periods" to assess whether China is following through on earlier commitments, including purchases of U.S. soybeans and other agricultural products and access to rare earths needed by American manufacturers.
"Whenever we have these compliance periods that roll over, it's a time for us to assess, reassess and determine whether or not to continue this period of relative peace on the economic front with the Chinese," Greer said.
Meanwhile, tariffs have sharply altered U.S. trade flows . Greer said Friday that the U.S. goods trade deficit with China has fallen nearly 40%, while acknowledging that some trade has shifted to other countries as companies adjust their supply chains.
Mexico has been one beneficiary of that shift. U.S. imports from Mexico reached a record $60.6 billion in July, according to the Census Bureau . The seasonally adjusted U.S. goods deficit with Mexico increased by $7.2 billion that month to $27.5 billion, according to the Census Bureau.
"When you impose tariffs ... you see market actors starting to do what market actors do, which is respond to new terms of trade, respond to new incentives in the market," Greer said. "We're actually seeing a lot come back to North America."
Greer's comments also provided new detail from the U.S. side following Trump's meeting with Xi at the White House on Thursday. Beijing has so far released a more detailed public account of the talks than Washington.
Xi told Trump on Thursday that artificial intelligence presents greater opportunities for U.S.-China cooperation than competition, according to a Chinese state media readout.
"The two sides can continue AI dialogue, exchange views on risks and benefits, and together guard against the misuse or malicious use of AI," Xi said, according to a CNBC translation of the readout .
Trump, in a Truth Social post Friday morning, called the meeting with Xi "very productive" and said the Chinese leader appeared receptive to Trump's preferred term of "SUPER INTELLIGENCE" for artificial intelligence.
"Tremendous things will be happening," Trump wrote.

One basis point is equal to 0.01%, and yields and prices move in opposite directions.

Donald Trump couldn’t help but offer guests at his state dinner with Chinese President Xi Jinping a first-ever tour of his ballroom construction site.
The president loves to boast to the White House press corps and his Truth Social followers about his passion projects around Washington, D.C ., especially the massive White House ballroom being built. Now, in front of an international audience, Trump has offered to share a glimpse of what he called a “clean and sparkly” construction site.
“And if I could go off script just for a second,” Trump said as dinner guests in the East Room of the White House laughed. “But as a special treat in honor of President Xi and Madame [Liyuan] Peng. I'd like to invite everyone in the room to visit through that beautiful curtain in the back.”
“It's one year away from completion — the new ballroom that you've heard about, and you will see something that I think you will really love.”
The 90,000-square-foot golden ballroom will fit 650 seats, compared to the 200 seats in the East Room. Trump has said construction will cost about $400 million and that he and other donors would pay for it.
But the project’s contractor told the administration that it would cost $600 million , with at least half expected to be covered by taxpayers, The Washington Post reported in June.
The Trump administration has also been challenged in court over whether it had the authority to tear down the East Wing last October to build the ballroom without Congressional approval. The Supreme Court ruled last month that the president can continue with construction for the time being .
“You'll be the first people to step foot on that, and we'll do that maybe after we're finished with the entertainment tonight. Anybody [who] wants to walk into a construction site that's nice and clean and sparkly, it's our honor to have you do so,” Trump told his dinner guests.
The official delegations from the US and China attended the state dinner. Some notable names on the guest list included first lady Melania Trump , Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio .
Trump was photographed next to Melania while waiting to greet Xi and his wife Peng at the White House ahead of the dinner. Makeup was caked on his left hand, which he often uses to cover up bruising .
The Trump administration has said the black and blue on the back of his hands is due to frequent handshaking and aspirin use .
Several of America’s tech leaders, such as SpaceX’s Elon Musk , OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg , were also in attendance Thursday night amid an AI race with China .
During the legal fight to build his ballroom, Trump argued that it was needed for national security. Underneath the East Wing sits a bunker dating back to 1942, after the U.S. entered World War II. In court filings, the Trump administration noted that bomb shelters, military installations and a medical facility would be added to the bunker during construction.
So when Trump suggested officials from China, an adversary of the U.S., tour the construction site, it raised some eyebrows.
“Of the security bunker? Seems suboptimal,” Reuters journalist Charlie Szymanski wrote on Bluesky.
“Guided tour of the super secure and classified military ballroom for officials of a foreign unfriendly nation. Totally reasonable,” another Bluesky user, Jeff Domingues, posted .
One X user wrote , “Let’s take the leader of China into the ballroom that doubles as a military bunker! Great idea Don!”
Melania led the preparations for the state dinner, which included a menu that the White House said had a “subtle Chinese influence.” For the main course, guests enjoyed sesame-crusted sea bass and braised baby bok choy.
Entertainment for the night was headlined by Christopher Macchio, a classically trained tenor who performed at Trump’s second inauguration. Guests were also treated to performances by military ensembles.
“Thank you, Mr. President and Mrs. Trump, for extending to my wife and me your gracious hospitality and thoughtful arrangements,” Xi said at the dinner through an interpreter. “You make us feel truly at home.”
“I would also like to extend my sincere greetings to Americans from all sectors of society who care about China-U.S. relations and support the further growth of our bilateral ties.”

articles.title_orig: Trump lavishes China's Xi during state visit. What did the summit accomplish?
articles.title_zh: Trump lavishes China's Xi during state visit. What did the summit accomplish?
articles.content_orig:
During remarks at the White House state dinner, Chinese President Xi Jinping said he and President Trump had "sincere and in-depth exchanges" earlier in the day, and "reached common understanding on many issues."
"This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability," Xi said through a translator.
Xi did not specify what the two leaders discussed or whether they struck any new agreements, but trade and AI were widely believed to be agenda items. The U.S. and China agreed earlier this week to extend a truce on tariffs for two months, forestalling another trade war for now, though the two countries have not struck a broader deal. The two sides are also rivals on advanced AI, with Mr. Trump arguing for light regulations in order to outpace China. Other major pressure points include China's relationships with Iran and Russia and the future of Taiwan.
Xi briefly recounted the history of U.S.-China ties. He pointed to President George Washington's purchase of Chinese porcelain , the two countries' cooperation during World War II and President Richard Nixon's moves to normalize relations with the People's Republic of China.
He said the U.S. and China have come to "another historic juncture," and argued the two countries' ambitions "can surely be mutually reinforcing."
"China and the United States must act as responsible major countries, meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other," he said.
President Trump gave his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, a large bald eagle sculpture at the end of his brief remarks at Thursday's state dinner.
During a speech recognizing U.S.-China ties, President Trump offered Chinese President Xi Jinping and other guests a "special treat" — a peek at the construction site for the White House ballroom.
"In honor of you, you'll be the first people to step foot on that," the president said, suggesting guests could take a look after the evening's entertainment wraps up.
Mr. Trump speaks about the ballroom frequently, weighing in on design decisions and casting the massive, controversial project as part of his legacy. He has often argued it will allow the White House to host larger state dinners.
"I can tell you that tonight, if we had it, we would've had way more than a thousand people [at the dinner] with standing room only," he said.
In remarks at Thursday's state dinner, President Trump called for the U.S. and China to "continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."
Mr. Trump, who has long touted his warm personal relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping, called Xi and his wife "truly outstanding, amazing people."
"As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure," Mr. Trump said. "And we've never gotten along better."
Mr. Trump traced the history of U.S.-China relations back to the European explorers who arrived at the American continent while scouring the Atlantic Ocean for new routes to China. He also pointed to early U.S. commercial ties with China, saying the two countries have exchanged "goods, knowledge, customs and ideas."
During a toast to Xi, he said: "May all of our people know a future of harmony, peace and success."
The White House released the invite list for Thursday's state dinner, which includes high-level government officials and several of the world's wealthiest tech executives.
Among the notable people on the guest list are Vice President JD Vance and several Cabinet-level officials: Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Attorney General Todd Blanche, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and CIA Director John Ratcliffe.
Mr. Trump's children – Ivanka, Eric and Tiffany – also got invites.
The world's richest person, Elon Musk, is on the list. NVIDIA's Jensen Huang, Meta's Mark Zuckerberg, Apple's Tim Cook, Google's Sundar Pichai, OpenAI's Sam Altman, Amazon's Jeff Bezos and TikTok investor Jeff Yass also got invites.
Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison is also attending. (Paramount Skydance is the parent company of CBS News.)
President Trump and first lady Melania Trump walked out of the White House's North Portico shortly after 7 p.m. Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife, Peng Liyuan, then arrived in a car and posed for photos with the Trumps before walking inside.
Mr. Trump did not answer shouted questions about Taiwan, Iran or whether Mr. Trump asked Xi to free imprisoned pro-democracy Hong Kong media tycoon Jimmy Lai .
A group of demonstrators was audible from the White House's North Portico ahead of Thursday evening's state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping.
A woman with a megaphone led a crowd of protesters through chants like: "Xi Jinping, You're Not Welcome," "Free Hong Kong," "Keep Taiwan Free" and "China Sponsors Genocide."
Jeff Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sanchez, have arrived at the White House state dinner.
Several minutes later, fellow tech titan Michael Dell and his wife, Susan, walked into the event.
Other high-profile executives are expected to attend the dinner, including the CEOs of Nvidia, Qualcomm and OpenAI, CBS News has previously reported.
Republican Sen. Thom Tillis questioned President Trump's judgment in hosting Chinese President Xi Jinping for a state dinner at the White House this week, saying he's "worried about the trend of spending more time with despots and less time with democratic leaders of nations."
"It's a WTF moment," the retiring North Carolina senator said in an interview with "CBS Evening News" anchor Tony Dokoupil on Thursday about Mr. Trump's red-carpet rollout for Xi compared to the reception that some U.S. allies like Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy have received.
"It's not that Xi Jinping is coming here to learn how to become a democratic, capitalist nation. Xi Jinping is trying to understand how his opposition will ultimately embrace their worldview," he said.
President Trump took to Truth Social to voice his frustration that CNN and MS NOW didn't air the arrival ceremony for Xi, saying it was "made for television." Other networks, including CBS News, also didn't air the arrival ceremony.
CNN and MS NOW, along with Politico, were banned from the White House last week. While a federal judge ordered the outlets' access to be restored, it's not clear whether CNN will be allowed to participate in the White House television pool . And as long as CNN lacks a guarantee that it will be in the regular pool rotation again, the other four networks that make up the pool also aren't participating.
Members of the pool — NBC, ABC, CBS, CNN and Fox News — are declining to provide video coverage of the president until the White House guarantees it will let CNN back in. Some networks chose not to air the government's feed of the event, since the television pool was not present. News outlets are still reporting on the event itself.
The arrival ceremony for Xi was not open to all media, but only to the pool. ABC News was the representative for the pool on Thursday.
"CNN and MSDNC, to show you how fake they are, today refused to cover one of the Biggest and Most Beautiful Events to take place in many years, the arrival at the White House of the Highly Respected President of China, Xi Jinping, and his beautiful wife, Madam Peng," Mr. Trump wrote. Olena Kalynychenko was looking forward to sharing the chrysanthemum tea she had bought in China with her partner.
“She said, ‘When I come back home, we will drink the tea made from Chinese flowers,’” said Oles Visich, Kalynychenko’s partner. He has now been waiting for news about her for a month, after she and thousands of others disappeared in catastrophic flooding along the Nepal-China border.
Her last known location was exiting China at a border post at 10:22 a.m. local time, 15 minutes before the flood.
Kalynychenko, 36, was part of a group of 56 people, mostly Ukrainians, who had traveled to Mount Kailash in Tibet for a spiritual retreat.
Their families' situation is a sign of how complex and time-consuming the process is of rescuing, recovering and identifying victims lost to the disaster. Given the number of missing, the process will likely take months.
They disappeared while heading from China to Nepal on their way home. Some relatives say they have received no information from authorities. The Chinese government has told at least two families that their relatives left Chinese territory before the flood struck, but they haven't been able to confirm whether they entered Nepal as Nepal's immigration complex and its records were destroyed in the floods.
The floods killed more than 1,400 people and left more than 6,000 missing, most of them on the Nepali side of the border. Nepal has said that 636 foreign nationals remain missing, including 54 Ukrainians. China has reported 261 foreign nationals among the missing on its side, including one Ukrainian.
Families in Ukraine say most of them have not received any answers since realizing their relatives were among the missing.
“We only have the statistics that are being posted online — how many people have been found, how many are alive, how many are dead, and how many are still missing,” said Stanislav Solohub, whose brother and sister-in-law went missing on Aug. 25.
Nepal says it has recovered 1,451 bodies, but only 112 have been handed over to families so far.
The government said it has collected DNA samples from 2,035 relatives so far, but it has not disclosed how many victims have been identified.
The group, led by Irina Blonskaya, a spiritual teacher who often organized retreats, was returning from its journey home in China when the flood struck Aug. 26. Their plan was to travel by bus from the Tibet region to Kathmandu , where its members would board flights to their respective countries. The group’s last message was sent at 8:27 a.m. Nepal time, about 10 minutes before the mountain slope collapsed.
Many had not checked in with their loved ones that morning, owing to the time difference.
Authorities have said the were triggered when a section of ice and rock broke away from a Himalayan mountain slope, creating a fast-moving torrent of water, ice, mud and debris. It destroyed communities and Gyirong Port, a border crossing used by some pilgrims traveling to or returning from Mount Kailash.
Vladsylava Horlova’s mother, Elena, was traveling in the group as well. She initially found her mother’s name of the list of the missing from the Nepali government, but hasn't received any further information from the Nepali side. Later, the Chinese embassy confirmed her mother had left the country, and was not counted in China's list of missing people.
Horlova, a college student who is a refugee in Norway , worries her mother wasn't in either country when the flood struck. There’s a stretch of road between the Nepali immigration building and the Chinese one along the border, videos from travelers show.
“You think about what if someone appeared to be in a no man’s land or that they left China, but not physically, who’s looking for them?” she asked.
Horlova has attempted to contact organizations ranging from the Ukrainian embassy in China, to Norwegian police, and even the Red Cross . She, like the others, have submitted their DNA samples to police to help the search.
On the other side of the border, China has said that when the remains of foreigners are identified, it will notify their respective embassies, but the authorities have not given any details about how many identities have been confirmed so far.
Though it has been a month since the original disaster, some families are still holding on to hope.
Just days before Kalynychenko left for her travels, she organized a retreat for women in Ukraine whose partners were fighting on the front lines of the war, some of whom had not heard from their partners for two years.
Visich, her partner, sees the irony of his situation, but like others in the group, has chosen to stay positive. Visich, also a psychologist, wrote a support guide for others like himself, offering tips on mental health.
“Because for my Olenka, for example, the most important thing in our connection, that each other … needs to be happy,” Visich said.
